summary: Research remaining cloud substrate domains across AWS/Google/Meta/Azure/Oracle; extend Oyatie decision matrix

research.domain: KMS + Secrets + HSM (key hierarchies, envelope encryption, BYOK/HYOK, HSM custody boundary, KMS availability architecture, key-use audit, crypto-shredding, secrets distribution, root-of-trust bootstrap)

per_company.approach: AWS KMS (+CloudHSM/XKS). Regional 'domains' of custom HSMs share daily-rotated 256-bit AES-GCM domain keys; a KMS key is a container over HSM backing keys (HBKs) generated on-HSM and NEVER exported in plaintext — exported only as Exported Key Tokens (EKTs) wrapped under domain keys into durable low-latency storage; per-encrypt derived keys exist only in HSM memory; customer data keys (CDKs) returned over TLS for envelope use, never stored by KMS. Rotation = new HBK version (yearly optional), old versions decrypt-only, zero data re-encryption; daily domain-key rotation rewraps EKTs (metadata-scale). Domain state changes are quorum-signed per-command (operators hold hardware tokens); HSMs never talk to each other — service hosts distribute signed domain tokens. Durability/one-way-door: 'no mechanism to export plaintext KMS keys'; offline HSMs + credentials stored in safes in multiple independent geographic locations, dual-control (1 security officer + 1 KMS operator from independent teams) + operator quorum to use. Availability: infrastructure in >=3 AZs/region, 99.999% monthly regional SLA (custom key stores/XKS excluded); quotas e.g. ~10k symmetric crypto ops/s/region (adjustable); ecosystem decouples from KMS hot path via Encryption SDK data-key caching and S3 Bucket Keys (up to 99% KMS request reduction). Multi-Region keys: same key ID + key material, fully independent per region. BYOK import (excluded from durability protections); HYOK via External Key Store with published open XKS proxy API spec — 250ms hard timeout, single retry, <=35ms ping guidance. Every key use logged in CloudTrail. Key deletion: mandatory 7–30 day waiting period.

Cloud KMS + Cloud HSM + Cloud EKM + Titan. Hierarchy: DEK → KEK (CMEK in Cloud KMS) → location-specific KMS master key in internal Keystore → Root Keystore master key; root keystore master key exists ONLY in RAM on a peer-to-peer fleet of dedicated 'master key distributor' machines (new instances fetch from running peers), with disaster backup on secure hardware in physical safes in multiple geographically distributed locations. Published hygiene cadence: KMS-master-key ciphertext max age 90 days, client-side cached keys max age 1 day, master keys refreshed every 24h, all customer keys re-encrypted monthly. Protection levels: SOFTWARE (FIPS 140-2 L1 modules), HSM (FIPS 140-2 L3, multi-tenant), HSM_SINGLE_TENANT; key material never seen decrypted by KMS API jobs. Key datastore: internal highly-available datastore with HMAC'd metadata, hourly integrity scans, 4-day change history, daily backups. EKM = HYOK (EXTERNAL / EXTERNAL_VPC); Key Access Justifications attaches justification codes + approve/deny policy to every external key access. Audit: Cloud Audit Logs + Access Transparency (logs of Google-employee actions) + internal request logs (no plaintext/ciphertext stored). Destruction: soft-delete (default 30 days, configurable destroy_scheduled_duration) + org-policy minimums. Titan chip = hardware root of trust measuring firmware/boot; sealed machine credentials released only if boot measurements satisfy policy (implicit attestation) — machine identity gates key release fleet-wide. Published KMS SLA historically only 99.5% (Encrypt/Decrypt/Sign) — Google leans on mandatory client-side DEK caching, not SLA headline.

Key Vault (multi-tenant; SLA raised to 99.99%; throttle ~2,000 HSM-key / 4,000 software-key GETs per 10s per vault) + Managed HSM ('key sovereignty'). Managed HSM pool = 3 instances on dedicated servers in separate racks, each with FIPS 140-3 L3 Marvell LiquidSecurity adapters hosting dozens of isolated partitions; each instance runs inside an Intel SGX TEE (Open Enclave SDK) handling TLS, requests, and access control; TEE-to-TEE 'attested TLS' pinned to the Managed HSM code-signing key (SGX platform reports signed by CPU-fused Intel keys); all service secrets sealed to per-CPU SGX sealing keys. Bootstrap: primary partition creates partition-owner root cert + DEK in HSM, syncs to secondaries over attested TLS; HSM-to-HSM data-wrapping key exchanged via vendor Diffie-Hellman API so even Microsoft service code only ferries opaque blobs. Security domain = blob (partition owner key, credentials, data-wrapping key, initial backup) protected by Shamir's Secret Sharing across customer-provided RSA keys with customer-chosen quorum — Microsoft personnel technically cannot access key material even with physical access; needed only on full-region loss. Confidential service healing auto-rebuilds failed instances with no customer action; blind backups wrapped by customer key; multi-region replication (6 synced instances) lifts SLA to 99.99% combined.

OCI Vault/KMS. Vault types: default (shared HSM partitions), Virtual Private Vault (dedicated isolated partition, 1,000 key versions included, only type with automatic rotation 60–365 days), Dedicated KMS (single-tenant: 3 auto-synchronized HSM partitions, PKCS#11 access), External KMS (HYOK, keys stay in third-party manager, only references in OCI). FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSMs, tamper-responsive (auto key-zeroize); HSM-protected MEKs non-exportable with all ops on-HSM; software-protected keys exportable but wrapped at rest by an HSM root key. Envelope encryption across Object Storage/Block Volume/File Storage/DB: services store only wrapped DEKs. Key versions under stable OCID; old versions decrypt-only; ciphertext self-identifies version (symmetric). BYOK via default 4096-bit RSA wrapping key. Availability: keys replicated across all 3 ADs (fault domains in single-AD regions), secrets across 2 ADs. Cross-region vault replication: automatic async copy, RTO near zero, RPO = 0 (primary doesn't ack success until key committed to persistent HSM storage); key material moves only as encrypted binary objects restored exclusively inside Oracle FIPS L3 HSMs. Deletion: 7–30 day waiting period; all usage in OCI Audit.

No general-purpose KMS product — identity-first PKI + derived keys + custody HSMs. Service encryption infra (2019): retired Kerberos (KDC lookups/thread pools couldn't survive bursty fan-out to thousands of peers); universal mutual TLS 1.3 (Fizz) with X.509; internal CA (ICA) issues three cert classes — high-privilege host certs, identity certs (service identity in custom X.509 extensions), low-privilege host certs; certs fetched at Tupperware container setup so issuance failure surfaces pre-deployment, removing the CA from the connection hot path; per-host unique certs enable individual audit + revocation; renewal = exchange-old-for-new only if not compromised. Session ticket keys (STEKs) are NOT distributed but deterministically derived: Generate_STEK(ica_secret, identity)=KDF(...) from 3 master keys, services hold prev/current/next versions — frequent rotation with zero cross-datacenter synchronization. Scale: thousands of services, hundreds of thousands of hosts, billions of requests/second; transport reliability 99.99% → 'almost 100%'. Custody HSMs at consumer scale: WhatsApp/Messenger E2EE backups use an HSM-based Backup Key Vault — HSM 'islands' replicate state via Raft across a fleet spanning >=7 datacenters with majority-consensus availability (2026 update: OTA key distribution + publicly verifiable deployment evidence). Deletion correctness: DELF framework (USENIX Security '20) — annotation-driven, asynchronous, temporarily-reversible deletions executing billions of deletions/day.

per_company.company: HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao (reference architecture; Oyatie already has OpenBao adapters)
per_company.approach: Single-binary secrets cell: 'barrier' encrypts everything before the storage backend; root key decrypts keyring/encryption key; default unseal = Shamir M-of-N key shares, or auto-unseal delegated to cloud KMS/HSM/transit engine of another Vault; seal-wrap for FIPS. Dynamic secrets: every issued credential gets a lease tracked by the expiration manager and auto-revoked at TTL — short-lived DB/cloud creds as first-class primitive. Deny-by-default ACL policies; audit devices record every request/response; Raft integrated storage for HA. Transit engine = encryption-as-a-service envelope wrap layer (also used as auto-unseal root for other clusters). OpenBao (Linux Foundation/OpenSSF, MPL-2.0, forked from Vault 1.14) is API-compatible and has mainlined former Enterprise features: namespaces (multi-tenancy), HSM/PKCS#11 auto-unseal, transform engine, horizontal read scalability on standbys.

convergent_patterns: Envelope encryption with a strict 3–4 level hierarchy everywhere: hardware-custodied root/domain key → versioned KEK/master key per tenant-or-purpose → per-object/per-chunk DEKs; data stores persist only wrapped DEKs adjacent to ciphertext (AWS HBK/EKT+CDK, GCP DEK→KEK→Keystore→Root Keystore, Azure double-wrapped key material, OCI MEK→DEK, Vault transit).

One-way door on key material: root and KEK plaintext never crosses the HSM/TEE boundary; everything that leaves is wrapped (AWS 'no mechanism to export plaintext KMS keys' + EKTs; OCI 'encrypted binary objects restored exclusively into FIPS L3 HSMs'; Azure SGX-sealed blobs; Google root key RAM-only). Decrypt happens by bringing ciphertext to the key, never the key to the data.

Rotation WITHOUT re-encryption via key versioning under a stable key identifier: new version encrypts forward, old versions retained decrypt-only, ciphertext self-describes its version (AWS HBK versions, GCP key versions + 90-day ciphertext age, OCI versions under constant OCID, Vault keyring). Only the thin wrap layer (EKTs / wrapped DEKs) is ever rewrapped in bulk.

Root-of-trust bootstrap is a quorum ceremony with offline/physical custody: AWS offline HSMs + credentials in safes at multiple sites under dual-control + quorum-signed domain commands with operator hardware tokens; Google root-key distributor in RAM with hardware backups in physical safes at multiple locations; Azure security domain Shamir-split across customer RSA keys; Vault/OpenBao Shamir M-of-N unseal. Nobody trusts a single human or a single site.

KMS availability is achieved by removing KMS from the hot path, not just by hardening KMS: client-side plaintext-DEK caching with bounded TTL (Google <=1 day; AWS Encryption SDK), hierarchical bucket-level keys (S3 Bucket Keys: up to 99% fewer KMS calls), and Meta's extreme form — deterministic KDF-derived STEKs and deploy-time cert issuance so NO central service is consulted at connection time.

Regional/cell independence as blast-radius boundary: keys are regional resources; cross-region capability is explicit, key-ID-preserving replication of wrapped material only (AWS Multi-Region keys, OCI replication with RPO=0 commit-before-ack, Azure Managed HSM 3+3 multi-region pools); no hyperscaler runs a synchronous global key plane.

Every single key use is audited to a centralized, tamper-evident log with caller identity and key version, and plaintext/ciphertext is never logged (CloudTrail; GCP triple lane — Cloud Audit Logs + Access Transparency for employee actions + internal request logs; Azure/OCI audit); operator actions get their own transparency lane.

Crypto-shredding is the deletion primitive, always with a mandatory waiting period and policy guardrails: AWS 7–30 days, GCP soft-delete default 30 days (org-policy minimums), OCI 7–30 days; per-tenant KEK destruction renders tenant data unrecoverable; Meta layers DELF-style deletion-correctness tooling on top (billions of deletions/day).

BYOK universally implemented as RSA-OAEP wrapping-key import; HYOK universally implemented as a brokered external-key call (AWS XKS, GCP EKM + Key Access Justifications, OCI External KMS) that is fenced with hard latency budgets (XKS: 250ms timeout, 1 retry, <=35ms ping) and EXCLUDED from the core availability SLA — external keys are a customer-accepted availability risk, never a core dependency.

Hardware HSMs are reserved for the root/wrap/custody layer; per-request bulk crypto runs in software FIPS modules or HSM-derived in-memory keys (Google SOFTWARE = FIPS L1 vs HSM = L3 tiers; Azure Key Vault software keys get 2x the throughput of HSM keys; Meta uses HSMs only for user-custody Backup Key Vault). HSM silicon throughput is treated as the scaling bottleneck it is.

Secrets distribution converged on short-lived, identity-derived credentials minted at workload placement, not static stored secrets: Meta certs issued at container setup with automatic exchange-renewal; cloud platforms' instance/workload identity → token exchange; Vault/OpenBao dynamic secrets with leases and automatic revocation; machine identity itself rooted in measured boot (Google Titan sealed credentials released only on policy-conforming measurements).

Quorum/multi-party authorization for every administrative action on key infrastructure: AWS per-command quorum-signed domain mutations; Azure customer RSA-key quorum for security-domain recovery; Google justification-gated approvals (KAJ); Vault Shamir thresholds — single-operator key administration does not exist at any of the five.
divergences: Published availability posture varies by 3 orders of magnitude: AWS commits 99.999%/region for KMS (flagship SLA, multi-AZ active-active), Azure Key Vault 99.99%, Google Cloud KMS published SLA historically just 99.5% — Google compensates architecturally (mandatory client DEK caching, 24h key refresh) rather than contractually.

Sovereignty mechanism: Azure is alone in using confidential computing (Intel SGX TEEs + attested TLS + CPU-sealed secrets) to make 'Microsoft cannot access keys' a technical property while keeping a fully managed SLA; AWS/Google/OCI achieve the equivalent with process controls (quorum ceremonies, access transparency, dual-custody safes).

HSM hardware strategy: AWS builds/operates its own custom KMS HSM appliances and a separate CloudHSM product; Azure buys Marvell LiquidSecurity (FIPS 140-3 L3) multi-partition adapters; OCI uses third-party FIPS 140-2 L3 partitions with a single-tenant Dedicated KMS tier; Google splits SOFTWARE (FIPS L1) vs HSM (L3) protection levels under one API; Meta builds HSM 'islands' coordinated by Raft for consumer key custody only.

Hierarchy root scope: Google roots EVERYTHING in one global internal Keystore/Root-KMS lineage (peer-to-peer RAM distributor + safes), while AWS deliberately keeps each region a fully independent cryptographic domain with its own offline-HSM durability story — global-efficiency vs regional-blast-radius philosophies.

Meta diverges entirely: no tenant-facing KMS; the platform problem is decomposed into (a) PKI-based workload identity at issuance time, (b) derived keys (KDF) instead of distributed keys, and (c) HSM custody only where users hold the secret (E2EE backups). Proof that an internal platform can skip a general-purpose KMS if identity + derivation are strong.

HYOK control point: GCP adds per-access human/policy approval semantics (Key Access Justifications with justification codes); AWS XKS is purely mechanical (latency-bounded proxy contract, published as an open spec); Azure/OCI sit between (external key references, no per-access justification protocol).

Multi-region semantics: AWS Multi-Region keys are symmetric peers (same key ID/material, independently usable); OCI is primary→replica with RPO=0 ack-on-commit; Azure Managed HSM extends one pool to 6 synced instances across two regions; Google keys are location-bound with no key-material replication story exposed at all.
anti_patterns: Central ticket/credential service on the connection hot path — Meta explicitly retired Kerberos because KDC lookups and thread pools collapsed under bursty fan-out; replaced with deploy-time certs + KDF-derived STEKs requiring zero runtime synchronization.

Static long-lived secrets in config/images/env — every player moved to issuance-time identity + leased short-lived credentials with automatic revocation (Vault leases, Meta cert exchange-renewal, cloud workload identity).

Any plaintext key export path, including for operators — AWS: 'There is no mechanism to export plaintext KMS keys'; Azure went further and removed Microsoft personnel from the trust boundary entirely via SGX. Operator break-glass access to key material is designed out, not policied out.

Calling KMS per object/request without DEK caching — S3 Bucket Keys exist precisely because per-object KMS calls melted cost and created availability coupling; Google enforces 1-day client cache TTLs as the norm.

Bulk data re-encryption on key rotation — universally avoided via versioned KEKs; only AWS domain-key rotation rewraps the thin EKT layer (metadata-scale). Re-encrypting data lakes on rotation is treated as a design failure.

Putting per-request crypto on HSM hardware — HSM partitions are the throughput bottleneck (Azure throughput is explicitly 'a function of underlying hardware capacity per partition'; HSM-key ops get half the rate limit of software keys); hardware is for custody/wrap, software for volume.

Synchronous cross-region key-plane dependencies — no hyperscaler has a global KMS data plane; regions/cells are independent failure domains, replication is explicit and asynchronous-with-commit-guarantees.
Core SLA dependency on external/customer-held keys — AWS excludes XKS/custom key stores from the 99.999% SLA and imposes a 250ms hard timeout; HYOK is fenced as a customer-accepted risk lane.

Immediate irreversible key deletion — every platform enforces a 7–30 day scheduled-deletion window with org-policy minimum enforcement; instant crypto-shred is considered an operator-error/ransomware amplifier.

Imported (BYOK) key material in the core durability story — AWS explicitly excludes imported material from durability protections (customer must retain a copy); durability promises only attach to service-generated keys.

HSM-to-HSM direct trust/communication — AWS HSMs never communicate directly; state flows as quorum-signed exported domain tokens via untrusted service hosts; Azure HSM partitions exchange wrap keys only via vendor DH APIs with service code ferrying opaque blobs. The transport is always untrusted.
oyatie_prescriptions: Build oya-kms as a single-concern Rust/axum service under the {oya,cloud}/<service>/ layout (ADR-0131/0132 compliant), cloning the AWS domain model: per-cell 'domain' of sealing roots → versioned per-tenant KEKs ('backing keys') stored ONLY as wrapped key tokens in the bespoke distributed-SQL store → per-object DEKs generated on demand and returned wrapped+plaintext over mTLS, never persisted by the KMS. Ciphertext headers carry key-ID + version so rotation is invisible to callers.

Enforce the one-way door in the type system from commit one: no API, trait, or debug path that returns root/KEK plaintext; KEK plaintext exists only inside a dedicated crypto-enclave process (separate binary, mlock'd + zeroize-on-drop via the zeroize crate, no swap, no core dumps); everything crossing the process boundary is a wrapped token. This is AWS's HBK/EKT discipline reimplemented Rust-native.

Rotation = append-only KEK versions under a stable key ID; old versions decrypt-only; never bulk re-encrypt tenant data; optional background rewrap-on-touch. Rotate cell domain keys on a fixed cadence (daily–weekly per AWS NIST SP 800-57 alignment) by rewrapping the key-token table only — design the token table so this is a metadata-scale batch job.

Mandatory per-tenant KEK for all SaaS data: tenant offboarding/GDPR = Cedar-gated, quorum-approved ScheduleKeyDeletion with a 7–30 day waiting period (default 30, org-policy minimum), then crypto-shred. Pair with a DELF-style deletion-correctness layer: deletion annotations on schema types in the distributed-SQL layer, asynchronous + temporarily reversible execution, so crypto-shred and row deletion are verified together.

Static stability doctrine (this is the highest-stakes item — KMS outage = everything outage): oya SDK caches plaintext DEKs with bounded TTL (<=24h, Google's ceiling) and the CAS object store uses bucket-key-style intermediate keys (S3 Bucket Keys pattern, 99% call reduction) so reads of already-keyed data NEVER require a live KMS call. KMS data plane is per-cell, multi-AZ, shuffle-sharded clients, constant-work request handling, no fallback paths (AWS doctrine). Publish 99.999% per-cell Encrypt/Decrypt SLO in {oya,cloud}/oya-kms/slos/*.openslo.yaml per ADR-0130 before promotion past dev.

Key authorization IS Cedar: key policies are Cedar policies attached to key resources, evaluated in the KMS request path with the policy-decision ID embedded in the audit record; model GCP Key Access Justifications as a Cedar condition on justification codes for the future HYOK lane. This unifies AWS key-policy semantics with the already-decided Oyatie policy engine instead of inventing a second authz language.

Audit every key use, no exceptions: every Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey/admin op emits a structured event (tenant, key ID+version, caller workload identity, Cedar decision ID, justification) into cloud/observability/ via Pulsar; never log plaintext or ciphertext; add a separate Access-Transparency-style lane for operator/automation actions on the KMS itself (Google's three-log split).

HSM boundary — be surgical: hardware custody ONLY for (a) cell domain/root keys and (b) future customer-custody products. W0–W2: OpenBao (existing adapters) as wrap layer + auto-unseal root, with PKCS#11 to a small pair of FIPS 140-3 L3 devices for root sealing. W5 bespoke destination: Rust enclave-replicated key service patterned on Azure Managed HSM — 3 replicas across racks/AZs, attested mTLS between replicas pinned to the Oyatie code-signing key (TPM/SEV-SNP measured-boot attestation from the Talos-style OS, Titan-pattern sealed credentials), secrets sealed to per-node hardware keys, confidential self-healing replacement of failed replicas. Do NOT route per-request crypto through HSM silicon.

Root-of-trust ceremony as a versioned runbook from day 0 (AWS durability model): Shamir M-of-N split of the offline root across hardware tokens held by independent officers; offline recovery material in two geographically separate safes under dual-control; ALL domain mutations (membership, quorum rules, rotation) are quorum-signed commands; replicas never trust each other directly — trust flows only through signed domain tokens, so the transport (k8s, Pulsar) stays untrusted.

Secrets distribution = identity, not secrets (Meta model, the strongest proven pattern): mint SPIFFE-style mTLS workload certs at pod admission via a bespoke Rust internal CA (cert fetch failure = deployment failure, pre-traffic), per-workload unique certs for audit/revocation, renewal as exchange-old-for-new; derive session-ticket-class and cache-class keys via KDF(ica_secret, identity, epoch) — prev/current/next versions — so rotation needs zero cross-cell synchronization; DB/Pulsar/service credentials are leased dynamic secrets (Vault lease semantics reimplemented Rust-native behind OpenBao API compatibility) with automatic expiry-revocation. Zero static secrets in images, env, or the buck2 delivery fabric.

Cell/region key independence: keys are cell-scoped resources; multi-cell keys are explicit replicas sharing key ID with wrapped-material-only transfer and OCI's commit-before-ack RPO=0 semantics; the KMS has no synchronous cross-cell runtime dependency, ever. The KMS cell is the unit AWS calls a 'domain' — align it with the existing cell-based + shuffle-sharding substrate.

BYOK/HYOK sequencing: launch BYOK with the universal RSA-OAEP wrapping-key import flow (exclude imported material from durability promises, AWS-style — customer retains a copy); defer HYOK to a fenced lane implementing the published AWS XKS proxy API spec as the contract (OpenBao/Vault already speak it), with a 250ms hard timeout + single retry and explicit exclusion from the core 99.999% SLO.

Bootstrap order for the dogfooded substrate: oya-kms must come up before the distributed-SQL store can decrypt its ranges — break the cycle the way Vault/Google do: KMS's own storage is a minimal local Raft group (not the main DB), unsealed via the ceremony root (OpenBao auto-unseal at W0, bespoke enclave quorum at W5), with the root key living only in RAM across a peer-distributor set (Google's distributor pattern) and safes as last-resort recovery.

research.domain: Network substrate + DNS + edge/CDN + load balancing (virtual network data plane, L4/L7 LB tiers, DNS static-stability doctrine, anycast/POP edge, east-west security, network control-plane dependency discipline)

per_company.approach: Nitro System: ALL VPC packet processing (encap/decap, security groups, routing, flow logs, DHCP/DNS) lives on dedicated Nitro cards, not host CPU or hypervisor — zero host cores burned, plus SRD multipath transport (ECMP spraying, out-of-order delivery, fast failover) for EFA/ENA Express. Hyperplane: one shared-state, cell-based, multi-tenant NFV fleet implements NLB, NAT Gateway, PrivateLink, EFS mounts, Lambda VPC ENIs — no per-customer LB instances; control plane scans DynamoDB and writes FULL config snapshots to S3, data plane periodically pulls (constant-work pattern, no event-driven deltas on critical path). Route 53: 2048 virtual name servers, every zone gets a shuffle shard of 4 with ≤2-NS overlap between any two zones (~730B possible shards), anycast from 50+ edge sites, the ONLY AWS service with a 100% data-plane availability SLA; control plane is single-region (us-east-1) by design — data plane never needs it. CloudFront: 750+ PoPs in 100+ cities, 1,140+ embedded PoPs inside ISP last-mile networks, 15 regional edge caches (three-tier cache); PoP selection is DNS-based, not HTTP anycast. Doctrine codified in Builders' Library: static stability, AZ independence (zonal data planes, in-zone traffic, NLB cross-zone off by default), control/data plane separation, ARC zonal shift for draining an AZ. Failure lesson: Oct 2025 us-east-1 outage — a race between three DNS 'Enactor' automation instances emptied the dynamodb.us-east-1 DNS record, cascading ~15 hours across dozens of services.

Andromeda (NSDI'18): host-software dataplane (OS-bypass userspace on Snap microkernel, SOSP'19) with a 300ns per-packet fast-path budget on a reserved core, coprocessor threads for heavy features, and the Hoverboard model — default flows are pre-programmed through shared gateways so the control plane is NEVER on flow-setup path; elephant flows get direct host-to-host offload (1.5M flows programmed in 1.9s/513MB vs 487M flows/74s/10GB pre-hoverboard, which capped networks at ~40K VMs). Maglev (NSDI'16): scale-out software L4 LB on commodity servers since 2008 — ECMP + BGP equal-weight VIP announcement, Maglev consistent hashing + minimal connection tracking, ~10Gbps small-packet line rate per machine. Two-tier serving: Maglev L4 → GFE L7 (TLS termination, buffering), one global anycast VIP steered by GSLB ('stabilized anycast'). B4 (SIGCOMM'13): SDN WAN with centralized TE running links near 100% utilization, 2–3x efficiency vs standard practice. Espresso (SIGCOMM'17): SDN peering edge carrying >22% of Google's internet egress, application-aware routing instead of big peering routers. Orion (NSDI'21): SDN control plane with explicit fail-static doctrine (data plane keeps forwarding on control-plane death), out-of-band control network to break circular dependencies, capability dependencies as a statically-checked DAG. Global VPC (single VPC spans all regions); Cloud DNS 100% availability SLA. East-west: ALTS since 2007 — workload-identity-bound (not host-bound) mutual auth, on by default zero-config for every RPC; evolving to PSP (open-sourced 2022) — stateless, UDP-encapsulated, NIC-offload-friendly encryption saving ~0.5% of fleet CPU. Internally NO Envoy sidecars: Stubby/gRPC routing as in-process library + GSLB; productized as proxyless gRPC xDS (Traffic Director/Cloud Service Mesh).

Katran (open source, prod since ~2017): L4 LB as XDP/eBPF program running BEFORE the kernel stack, co-located on backend servers in PoPs (no dedicated LB tier), extended Maglev hashing, DSR via IPIP encap, no cross-node state sync. L7: proxygen (open-sourced HTTP stack) + mvfst (QUIC) + Fizz (TLS 1.3) at edge PoPs; DNS dynamically maps each user to a nearby PoP balancing load (CACM 2025 'Meta's Hyperscale Infrastructure') — DNS-steered unicast, not HTTP anycast. Backbone split into two networks: classic internet-facing backbone + Express Backbone (EBB, SIGCOMM'23) — dedicated cross-DC SD-WAN with central traffic engineering + Open/R distributed routing; Edge Fabric (SIGCOMM'17) does SDN egress TE at PoPs (their Espresso analog). FBOSS: own switch OS on own switch hardware. ServiceRouter (OSDI'23): global service mesh since 2012 implemented as a LIBRARY linked into service binaries — 99% of RPCs routed client→server directly with no proxy hop, only 1% via sidecar/remote proxies; millions of L7 routers routing tens of billions of requests; the library design 'saves hundreds of thousands of machines' vs sidecar mesh. Failure lesson: Oct 4 2021 — backbone maintenance command + audit-tool bug disconnected all DCs; DNS servers were designed to withdraw their anycast BGP routes when they couldn't reach DCs, so DNS took itself off the internet and internal tooling (which depended on the same DNS/network) was locked out for ~6 hours.

VFP (NSDI'17): programmable virtual switch with layered match-action tables on every Azure host (1M+ hosts) — the single SDN enforcement point for VNETs, ACLs, NAT, LB. AccelNet (NSDI'18): FPGA SmartNIC as bump-in-the-wire between NIC and ToR since 2015 — first packet of a flow goes through VFP software, then the flow is offloaded to the FPGA's Generic Flow Table for hardware forwarding; Microsoft explicitly rejected ASICs (1–2yr silicon cycles vs 5yr server life = no feature velocity) and CPU-core dataplanes (cost/power at 40GbE+); built with <5 FPGA developers. Ananta lineage software L4 LB; SONiC: Azure's open-sourced datacenter switch OS, now industry standard. Azure Front Door: 150+ PoPs, anycast for DNS + HTTP, split TCP (terminate client TCP/TLS at PoP, pre-established reused origin connections), PoPs organized in primary/fallback rings — notably MIGRATING from anycast to unicast (DNS-steered) PoP selection through March–April 2026. Azure DNS: 100% availability SLA for valid DNS requests, 4 anycast name servers per zone (delegation to all 4 required for SLA).

Off-box virtualization: OCI's founding differentiator — network virtualization runs on dedicated devices OUTSIDE the host (predating the DPU trend), so hypervisor/host carry no network virtualization stack; enables bare-metal instances with full isolation ('Isolated Network Virtualization' security posture: compromised host cannot attack the network). Flat VCN design: no routing between subnets — virtualization stack answers pre-canned ARP, all vNICs in the overlay communicate directly; physical fabric is a non-oversubscribed Clos with a published guaranteed maximum of TWO hops between any hosts in an AD (predictable low latency is the marketed contract; OCI uniquely publishes network performance SLAs alongside availability/manageability SLAs). Cluster networks: dedicated RoCEv2 RDMA fabric over NVIDIA ConnectX SmartNICs, purpose-built and NOT shared with non-RDMA traffic — basis of their GPU supercluster pitch. Newer Acceleron NIC work continues the off-box/host-offload line. OCI DNS: global anycast authoritative DNS; regions split into Availability Domains and Fault Domains as the published fault-isolation hierarchy. Less published peer-reviewed detail than the other four — treat quantitative marketing claims (e.g., microsecond-class VCN latency) as vendor claims, while the two-hop flat Clos and off-box architecture are well documented first-principles posts.

convergent_patterns: Get packet processing OFF the general-purpose host kernel path — all five converged, differing only in substrate: dedicated hardware cards (AWS Nitro), FPGA SmartNIC (Azure AccelNet), off-box devices (OCI), OS-bypass userspace + NIC offloads (Google Andromeda/Snap), XDP-before-kernel (Meta Katran). Nobody at scale runs the data plane through the stock kernel network stack.

L4 load balancing is scale-out software on commodity servers with BGP/ECMP anycast VIPs + consistent hashing (Maglev hash family) + minimal local connection state + DSR/tunnel return — Google Maglev, Meta Katran, Azure Ananta/SLB, AWS Hyperplane all replaced hardware LB appliances with this exact shape; capacity scales by adding machines, failures redistribute via consistent hashing not state-sync.

Two-tier LB split: stateless-ish L4 anycast/ECMP tier → stateful L7 TLS-terminating proxy tier (Maglev→GFE, Katran→proxygen, Front Door L4→L7 at PoP, NLB/Hyperplane→ALB). TLS/HTTP intelligence never lives in the L4 tier.

DNS is the most-available service in the company, engineered to a 100% SLA: Route 53, Azure DNS, and Google Cloud DNS all carry 100% availability SLAs; all serve via global anycast; AWS and Azure both delegate exactly 4 name servers per zone from fault-isolated pools (Route 53: shuffle shard of 4 from 2048 virtual NS, ≤2-NS overlap between zones). DNS data plane must operate indefinitely without its control plane.

Strict control-plane/data-plane separation + fail-static doctrine: data plane continues forwarding from last-known-good state when the control plane is dead (Orion fail-static, AWS static stability, Hyperplane pull-from-S3, hoverboard pre-programmed defaults). Corollary all converged on: the control plane is NEVER on the packet/flow-setup critical path.

Constant-work config distribution: push/pull COMPLETE versioned state snapshots at a fixed cadence rather than event-driven deltas (Route 53 + Hyperplane DynamoDB→S3 full-file pattern; hoverboard default programming) — workload is identical in calm and storm, so storms can't overload the propagation path.

Cell-based multi-tenant shared fleets with shuffle sharding for blast-radius control: Hyperplane cells back NLB/NAT/PrivateLink for all customers; Route 53 shuffle shards isolate DDoS to 4 virtual NS plus dedicated attack capacity; Front Door primary/fallback rings. No per-tenant dedicated network appliances.

No sidecar proxies in their own fleets — mesh-as-library: Meta ServiceRouter routes 99% of RPCs via a library linked into the binary (saving hundreds of thousands of machines); Google's internal Stubby+GSLB+ALTS is in-process and their cloud push is proxyless gRPC xDS; AWS internally uses SDK+ELB and is sunsetting App Mesh; even Istio itself retired the sidecar model (ambient mode GA 1.24). Sidecar-per-pod is a pattern hyperscalers sell-adjacent but do not run.

East-west authentication/encryption bound to WORKLOAD identity (not host/IP), on by default with zero app config, terminated below or beside the app in platform code, with a roadmap to stateless NIC offload (Google ALTS→PSP; AWS transparent Nitro-layer VPC encryption; Meta fleet-wide TLS 1.3 via Fizz).

Own the switch/routing software layer (SDN) with centralized traffic engineering once you own fabric: Google B4/Espresso/Orion, Meta FBOSS/Open/R/EBB/Edge Fabric, Azure SONiC, AWS custom routers — and run WAN links hot (B4 near-100% utilization) only because central TE + fail-static makes it safe.

Every fault domain is drainable as a first-class, fast, data-plane-only operation: AWS ARC zonal shift, Meta routinely drains PoPs (Edge Fabric/DNS steering), Google GSLB drains clusters, Front Door fallback rings. Recovery = shift traffic, not reconfigure systems.
divergences: VPC scope: Google is alone with a global VPC (one network spans all regions, global routes/firewalls); AWS, Azure, OCI are regional-VPC with explicit peering/transit — AWS argues regionality is a fault-isolation feature (region = blast-radius boundary).

Edge steering: HTTP anycast (Google single global VIP, Azure Front Door classic) vs DNS-steered unicast PoP mapping (CloudFront, Meta) — and Azure Front Door is actively migrating anycast→unicast in 2026, suggesting DNS-steered mapping won on controllability/drain precision for L7 edge; anycast remains universal for DNS itself.

Host dataplane substrate: custom ASIC cards (AWS Nitro), FPGA for velocity (Azure — explicitly rejected ASIC timelines), off-box appliance (OCI), software-on-host-CPU with selective offload (Google — argues feature velocity + isolation, accepts burning a core). No consensus on the hardware; total consensus on the abstraction (flow-table offload + software slow path).

LB state philosophy: Hyperplane is a shared-state cell fabric (flow state replicated within a cell, enabling NAT/stateful NFV); Maglev/Katran minimize state (consistent hashing primary, local-only connection table) and accept rare resets. Stateful-by-design vs stateless-by-design at L4.

WAN philosophy: Google and Meta run dual backbones (user-facing vs inter-DC) with centralized TE at near-100% utilization; AWS/Azure/OCI publish far less and appear to run more conventional overprovisioned WANs (cold-potato global networks) without claiming hot-link TE economics.

OCI's flat L2-illusion VCN (no inter-subnet routing hops, pre-canned ARP, 2-hop guarantee) vs everyone else's routed overlay — OCI trades generality for latency predictability and lift-and-shift compatibility.

East-west crypto layer: application-layer protocol with custom handshake (Google ALTS), standard TLS 1.3 in-library (Meta Fizz), transparent infrastructure-layer encryption invisible to workloads (AWS Nitro VPC encryption) — identity-bound principle converged, the layer did not.

Mesh productization vs internal reality: Google/AWS/Azure sell sidecar meshes (Istio/ASM, App Mesh→retired, OSM→retired) while running libraries internally; Meta published the gap explicitly (1% proxy / 99% library).
anti_patterns: Hardware load-balancer appliances: explicitly replaced by all (Maglev 2008, Azure Ananta, Meta moved IPVS→Katran) — capacity ratchets, pair-failover blast radius, no incremental scale-out.

Per-pod sidecar proxies at fleet scale: Meta quantified the cost (library model saves hundreds of thousands of machines); Istio itself deprecated the model into ambient/ztunnel; AWS announced App Mesh end-of-support (Sept 2026) and Azure retired OSM. Sidecars are a retired pattern at hyperscale.

On-demand/reactive flow setup with the control plane on the critical path (classic OpenFlow model): Andromeda's hoverboard exists precisely because pre-programming all-pairs flows OR setting up flows on demand both failed (~40K-VM ceiling, 74s programming); default routes must be statically pre-programmed.

Health/advertisement automation that can converge to zero: Meta 2021 (DNS servers withdrew their own anycast routes when the backbone died, taking the recovery tooling with them) and AWS Oct 2025 (DNS Enactor race emptied dynamodb.us-east-1's record). Lesson both published: automation must have a floor — never withdraw/delete the last viable answer; fail static instead.

In-band control planes with circular dependencies on the network they control: Orion mandates out-of-band control network + statically-verified DAG of capability dependencies (no loops); Meta's internal tools depending on production DNS/backbone is the canonical failure.
Event-driven delta config propagation for critical data planes: replaced by constant-work full-snapshot push (AWS Builders' Library) because delta pipelines fall behind exactly during incidents.

Burning general-purpose host cores on packet processing (AWS sells those cores; Azure judged CPU dataplanes too costly at 40GbE+) and ASIC-only dataplanes (Azure: 1–2yr silicon cycles kill feature velocity) — the converged escape is programmable offload with a software exception path.

Cross-AZ data-path traffic by default: AWS AZ-independence pattern keeps traffic in-zone (NLB cross-zone off by default); cross-zone hops add cost, latency, and turn zonal failures into regional ones.
Dedicated per-customer network appliance instances: Hyperplane's multi-tenant shared cells replaced the dedicated-instance model (waste + cold-start + uneven blast radius).

DNS geolocation guessing as the only steering signal: Google built stabilized anycast + GSLB, Meta builds measurement-driven PoP maps — naive resolver-location DNS steering alone is insufficient (though DNS-steered unicast with good mapping is winning over raw anycast for L7).
oyatie_prescriptions: L4 tier = Rust Katran-equivalent: eBPF/XDP dataplane authored with aya (Rust eBPF toolchain), Maglev consistent hashing, local-only connection table (no cross-node state sync), DSR via IPIP/GUE encap, VIPs announced via BGP/ECMP from each cell; co-locate on workload nodes Meta-style to avoid a dedicated LB fleet at launch scale. This is the proven shape at 3+ hyperscalers — do not build a stateful Hyperplane-style shared-state fabric until NAT/PrivateLink-class features demand it.

L7 tier = Rust GFE/proxygen-equivalent built on hyper/tower (axum lineage): TLS termination (rustls), h2 + h3 (s2n-quic or quiche), split-TCP with pre-established reused origin connection pools, request buffering, and GSLB-style weighted cell selection. Keep ALL L7 intelligence out of the L4 tier.

DNS is W0-critical substrate, engineered to the Route 53 doctrine: bespoke Rust authoritative server (hickory-dns as reference, bespoke per founder doctrine); 2048-virtual-NS / shuffle-shard-of-4 per tenant zone with ≤2-NS overlap (port Route 53 Infima's algorithm to Rust); anycast announcement from every cell; data plane serves exclusively from complete, versioned, signed zone snapshots pulled from the bespoke CAS object store — it must run forever with the control plane dead. Hard invariant enforced in code: no automation may ever produce an empty/below-floor record set (codify the AWS Oct-2025 and Meta Oct-2021 lessons as a minimum-viable-answer floor + 'DNS never withdraws its own reachability based on backend health').

Control/data plane separation as a repo-level architectural rule (fits ADR-0131 single-concern layout): every cloud/<network-service>/ ships two single-concern services — a config compiler (control) that publishes complete content-addressed snapshots into the CAS delivery fabric, and a Rust dataplane that pulls/verifies/atomically-swaps and FAILS STATIC on staleness. Constant-work cadence (fixed-interval full-snapshot fetch), never event-driven deltas on the critical path. This composes naturally with buck2 + content-addressed delivery.

Virtual network dataplane: follow Google's software path (no custom silicon available): hoverboard model — pre-program default routes through shared gateway cells so the SDN control plane is never on flow-setup path; detect elephant flows and install direct host-to-host offload entries; structure the host dataplane as ns-budgeted fast path + coprocessor threads for heavy features (Andromeda's 300ns budget discipline). On Talos-class owned OS, implement as XDP/AF_XDP Rust dataplane; design the flow-table abstraction (GFT/VFP-style layered match-action) so a future DPU offload is a backend swap, not a rewrite.

NO sidecars — mesh as a Rust library (the ServiceRouter/Stubby model, now proven by Meta's published 99%-library economics and Istio's own retreat): a tower middleware stack linked into every axum service providing discovery, weighted/locality-aware LB, retries/hedging/outlier ejection, drains, and telemetry, driven by an xDS-compatible Rust control plane; keep a tiny proxy fleet (~1% of traffic) only for non-Rust/external/legacy callers. Cedar authorization evaluates in-process in the same middleware — no policy sidecar.

East-west security = ALTS model reimplemented in Rust: workload-identity-bound credentials (identity = service/workload, never host/IP; issued by the owned CA from the k8s/Talos attestation chain), mutual auth + encryption on by default zero-config inside the RPC library. Choose a PSP-shaped wire format (stateless, UDP-encapsulated, per-connection derivable keys, offload-friendly — Google open-sourced the spec) so NIC offload is a later drop-in.

Cells + shuffle sharding for every multi-tenant network service (already Oyatie doctrine — apply it to network substrate specifically): multi-tenant LB/NAT/ingress cells, per-tenant shuffle-shard assignment, plus pre-provisioned dedicated 'attack capacity' cells DDoS traffic can be shifted into (Route 53's pattern).

Zonal independence + drainability: one k8s cluster (Cluster API) per zone/cell, never spanning fault domains; zonal service endpoints; data-path traffic stays in-zone by default with cross-zone only at the L7 routing tier under explicit budget; ship 'zonal shift' as a first-class data-plane-only API from day one (ARC zonal shift / Meta PoP drain semantics: shift traffic in seconds without touching config of the impaired zone). Statically pre-provision N+1 zone capacity so recovery never depends on control planes (AWS static stability).

Edge/POP architecture: DNS-steered unicast PoP selection (the CloudFront/Meta model, and where Azure Front Door is converging in 2026) with measurement-driven mapping; anycast reserved for the DNS tier itself; QUIC+split-TCP termination at PoPs with pre-warmed origin pools; when CDN ships, adopt CloudFront's three-tier cache topology (PoP → regional shield → origin) for cache hit ratio + origin protection.

Break control-plane circular dependencies structurally (Orion doctrine): management/control traffic on an out-of-band path that does not traverse the dataplane it programs; express inter-service capability dependencies as a DAG statically checked in CI (buck2 query can enforce acyclicity); every network control plane must list its own dependencies and provably exclude the services it serves (the bespoke distributed-SQL store must not sit under the DNS/LB dataplane's serving path — snapshots from CAS only).

Run the substrate roadmap in proven order: L4 LB + authoritative DNS + L7 proxy + mesh-library are W-now (all five companies' first-decade investments); SDN WAN/TE (B4/EBB-class) and switch OS (SONiC/FBOSS-class) only when Oyatie owns physical fabric — until then encode fabric intent in OpenTofu and keep the Orion-style intent model as the API boundary so hardware ownership is a backend change.

research.domain: Data substrate — operational databases (distributed SQL/NoSQL, storage engines, clocks, tenant isolation, CDC, DB control planes); feeds Oyatie W5 bespoke distributed-SQL (Spanner/CRDB-class, multi-Raft leader-per-range, ratified anchor)

per_company.approach: Aurora (SIGMOD'17 'log is the database'): compute/storage disaggregation; redo log records are the only thing crossing the network; storage layer materializes pages asynchronously; 6 copies across 3 AZs in 10GB protection groups, 4/6 write quorum, 3/6 read quorum; 35x more transactions than mirrored MySQL and ~7.7x fewer I/Os per transaction in published tests; continuous backup = streaming log archival to S3 with PITR. Aurora SIGMOD'18 explicitly avoids distributed consensus on the I/O path (quorum sets + epochs instead of Paxos per write); segment repair restores a 10GB segment in ~10s. Control plane: RDS for instance orchestration; the storage control plane persists volume metadata in DynamoDB and recovers via S3 — i.e., the DB control plane is built on a simpler database. DynamoDB (USENIX ATC'22): partitions replicated by multi-Paxos with a leader per partition (NOT the leaderless 2007 Dynamo); replicas hold B-tree + WAL; log-only (witness) replicas cut quorum cost; token-bucket admission at table+partition; adaptive capacity eliminated 99.99% of skew throttling, then was replaced by proactive Global Admission Control (GAC); split-for-heat partition management by AutoAdmin; MemDS constant-work metadata/routing service (Perkle trie) to kill metastable cache-miss storms; per-second PITR to any point in 35 days via continuous log archival; Prime Day 2024: 146M req/s peak at single-digit-ms latency, tens of trillions of API calls. Aurora DSQL (re:Invent 2024): active-active multi-region OCC SQL using microsecond-bounded Amazon Time Sync clocks, 99.999% multi-region availability target — AWS converging on Spanner-style bounded-uncertainty clocks as commodity.

Spanner (OSDI'12): data sharded into splits; one Paxos group per split (leader-per-range archetype); 2PC layered over Paxos groups for cross-split transactions; TrueTime (GPS + atomic-clock armageddon masters) exposes bounded clock uncertainty epsilon (avg ~4ms, 1–7ms sawtooth in the paper) and commit-wait yields external consistency — first system to provide it at global scale; lock-free snapshot reads at any replica; exact-staleness/bounded-staleness read classes. Production scale (Google Cloud blog, Spanner-in-2025): >6B queries/sec at peak, >17 exabytes under management (up from 2B/6EB in 2022). Storage engine migrated online, fleet-wide, from Bigtable-style SSTable stack to Ressi (columnar-block LSM) with zero downtime — proof that planet-scale engine swaps are operationally tractable. F1 (VLDB'13) online asynchronous schema change: multi-phase delete-only → write-only → backfill → public protocol; proves naive distributed DDL corrupts data and gives the correctness model everyone copied. Schema changes in Spanner are non-blocking and use TrueTime timestamps. Change streams are DDL-level schema objects; change records are written in the same transaction and co-located with the data write. Bigtable: single tablet server per tablet over Colossus (replication delegated to the filesystem), >10 exabytes under management, load-based tablet splitting.

Per-use-case bespoke stores over a shared MySQL+RocksDB substrate, no public cloud. TAO (USENIX ATC'13): write-through graph cache over sharded MySQL; >1B reads/s and millions of writes/s on thousands of machines; read-after-write consistency per region via write-through design; petabytes of social graph. UDB MySQL fleet: MyRocks (VLDB'20) — LSM storage engine on RocksDB inside MySQL; migration cut instance size 62.3% vs compressed InnoDB (50% fleet storage) and reduced flash write traffic ~75%; fleet-wide UDB migration completed 2017 with zero-downtime instance-by-instance copy — the canonical proven LSM-over-B-tree result. OnlineSchemaChange (OSC, open-sourced; rebuilt in Python 2017): shadow-table copy + changelog capture + atomic swap; fleet-wide schema change went from ~6 months to ~half a day. ZippyDB (Meta eng blog 2021): largest strongly consistent geo-distributed KV store at Meta; RocksDB shards replicated via Data Shuttle using Paxos (or async per config); primary + followers + witness-style configs; keyspace partitioned into μshards (tens of thousands per physical shard); Akkio places μshards near access locality instead of replicating everywhere. Wormhole (NSDI'15): binlog-tailing pub-sub CDC as platform primitive feeding caches/indexes/warehouses.

Cosmos DB: globally distributed multi-model DB; per physical partition a leader-based replica set (typically 4 replicas, dynamic quorum reconfiguration); five precisely specified consistency levels (strong, bounded staleness K-versions/T-time, session, consistent prefix, eventual); multi-region (multi-master) writes with LWW or custom conflict resolution — strong consistency unavailable in multi-write mode; financially backed SLAs: P99 <10ms point read AND <10ms write, 99.999% read availability for multi-region accounts; Request Unit (RU) normalized-cost admission control as the tenant-isolation currency; change feed as built-in CDC primitive; heat-based partition splitting. Azure SQL Hyperscale / Socrates (SIGMOD'19): Aurora-class log disaggregation — separates durability (log service, 'XLOG') from availability (page servers), compute scales independently of 100TB+ storage; second independent confirmation of log-is-the-database. Hyperscale (Citus) (SIGMOD'21): coordinator + workers sharding as a PostgreSQL extension — distributed Postgres without forking the engine; Microsoft's pragmatic alternative lane for relational scale-out.

Opposite pole: shared-storage scale-up with hardware-assisted predictability instead of shared-nothing ranges. Exadata: RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) fabric between DB servers and intelligent storage servers; XRMEM (RDMA-accessible memory tier in storage) gives 8K OLTP read I/O as low as 14μs on X11M (sub-19μs on X9M) by bypassing OS/network stacks; Smart Scan offloads predicate evaluation/columnarization to storage CPUs; tiered XRMEM→flash→HDD auto-caching. RAC shared-disk clustering for scale-out within the shared-volume model. Autonomous Database: CDB/PDB (container/pluggable) multitenancy on dedicated Exadata; control-plane servers are the secure-tunnel gateway that orchestrate cloud automation, telemetry routing, and patch-image hosting; ML-driven automated patching/upgrade/tuning/scaling executed online without human intervention; Fleet Patching & Provisioning moves PDBs between CDBs for fleet maintenance; Data Guard physical standby for DR, automatic continuous backups for PITR. Proven for lift-and-shift enterprise Oracle workloads; not a shared-nothing horizontal-scale reference.

convergent_patterns: Leader-per-partition consensus replication is the universal endpoint: Spanner (Paxos group per split), DynamoDB (multi-Paxos leader per partition), CockroachDB/TiKV (Raft group per range), Cosmos DB (leader-based replica set per partition), ZippyDB (Paxos per shard). Every hyperscaler that started leaderless or single-leader converged here; the range/partition is simultaneously the unit of consensus, placement, splitting, and repair.

Heat-based automatic splitting + rebalancing driven by a dedicated placement/fleet-management service: DynamoDB AutoAdmin split-for-heat, Spanner load-based splitting, Bigtable tablet splits, TiKV Placement Driver, Cosmos partition splits. Static hash-sharding without an online re-placement brain is universally insufficient.

Tenant isolation in shared fleets via normalized-cost token-bucket admission control at BOTH the request-router layer and the partition layer, trending from reactive (DynamoDB adaptive capacity) to proactive global coordination (GAC); Cosmos RUs and DynamoDB RCU/WCU are the same idea. Per-tenant dedicated clusters are the exception (Oracle dedicated Exadata), not the default.

LSM-tree (RocksDB lineage) as the operational storage engine: MyRocks/ZippyDB/TAO-backing (RocksDB), TiKV (RocksDB + Raft Engine), CockroachDB (RocksDB then Pebble clean-room rewrite), Spanner Ressi (columnar LSM). Published Meta numbers: 50% space, ~75% less write traffic vs compressed InnoDB. (Sole counterexample: DynamoDB B-tree replicas.)

Log-centric disaggregated storage independently invented 3x: Aurora (log is the database, 4/6 quorum), Azure Socrates (XLOG + page servers), Google AlloyDB; Oracle Exadata achieves the same goal (storage that understands the database) via hardware offload. Only the log crosses the network; pages/SSTs materialize asynchronously.

Bounded-uncertainty timestamps as the transaction-ordering substrate: TrueTime epsilon + commit-wait (Spanner), HLC + uncertainty-interval restarts with NTP-grade clocks (CockroachDB, max-offset 500ms default), microsecond-bounded Amazon Time Sync driving Aurora DSQL. The TrueTime API shape (interval, not instant) won; the atomic-clock hardware is now optional and increasingly commodity.

Online multi-phase asynchronous schema change is non-negotiable: F1 protocol (delete-only → write-only → backfill → public) adopted by Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB; Meta achieves the same property operationally via OSC shadow-copy. No hyperscaler tolerates blocking DDL on a production fleet.

CDC as a first-class, transactionally-consistent platform primitive co-located with the write path: DynamoDB Streams (shards split with partitions), Spanner change streams (DDL objects, change record written in the same transaction), Cosmos change feed, Meta Wormhole binlog tailing. Downstream caches, indexes, search, and warehouses all hang off it.

Continuous log archival to object storage giving per-second PITR with ~35-day windows: DynamoDB PITR (any second, 1–35 days), Aurora (redo streamed to S3), Cosmos continuous backup, Oracle automatic backup + redo shipping. Backup is a property of the log pipeline, not a periodic job.

The managed-DB control plane is a separate, smaller, simpler stateful system: Aurora storage control plane persists in DynamoDB + S3; AutoAdmin manages DynamoDB; Oracle control-plane servers orchestrate Autonomous fleets. Control planes are cell-scoped, do failure-driven repair (gossip/epoch-based), and never sit on the data path.

Predictability over peak performance as explicit doctrine: DynamoDB ATC'22 frames the whole service around 'predictable performance'; Cosmos backs P99 <10ms with financial SLAs; Exadata buys determinism with RDMA; MemDS is deliberately constant-work so cache state cannot change system behavior.
divergences: Clock infrastructure: Google requires owned hardware (GPS + atomic clocks, epsilon ~1–7ms) and pays commit-wait for external consistency; CockroachDB refuses special hardware and pays uncertainty-restarts + no strict external consistency; TiDB centralizes timestamps in a TSO (PD) and pays a round-trip + single-region bias; AWS DSQL splits the difference with microsecond-bounded fleet time-sync.

Shared-nothing range-sharded (Spanner, DynamoDB, CockroachDB, TiKV, ZippyDB) vs shared-storage scale-up/out (Oracle Exadata RAC, Aurora single-writer shared volume, Azure Hyperscale). The shared-storage camp wins single-writer relational compatibility and lift-and-shift; the shared-nothing camp wins horizontal write scale.

Cross-region write topology: Spanner accepts WAN commit latency for one true external-consistency timeline; Cosmos DB and DynamoDB global tables accept LWW/custom conflict resolution for local-region write latency (and Cosmos drops strong consistency entirely in multi-write mode).

Consistency surface philosophy: Cosmos exposes five user-tunable levels as product; Spanner/CockroachDB ship one strong default and expose only read-time staleness knobs; Meta gives each internal use case a differently-tuned bespoke store (TAO async, ZippyDB per-config Paxos vs async).

Read scaling: Meta fronts the database with a giant write-through cache tier (TAO, 1B+ reads/s) and accepts cache-consistency machinery; cloud vendors push reads into the replication layer itself (Aurora replicas off shared storage, Spanner follower/staleness reads).

Storage engine: DynamoDB stayed B-tree+WAL per replica (point-op predictability) while Google/Meta/CRDB/TiKV all standardized on LSM; both are proven, but LSM won everywhere space/write-amplification dominates cost.

Buy-vs-build inside the company: Meta runs thousands of MySQL primaries with external orchestration and per-use-case stores; Google built one general database and forced workloads onto it; Oracle bets on vertically-integrated hardware. All three are proven — the divergence is organizational, not technical.
anti_patterns: Leaderless eventually-consistent quorums (the 2007 Dynamo design): Amazon itself retired it — DynamoDB-the-service (2012+, ATC'22) is leader-based multi-Paxos because divergence reconciliation and unpredictable latency were operationally toxic.

Distributed consensus on the storage I/O hot path: Aurora SIGMOD'18 is literally titled 'On Avoiding Distributed Consensus for I/Os, Commits, and Membership Changes' — quorum sets + epochs, consensus reserved for rare reconfiguration.

Reactive, best-effort hot-partition handling: DynamoDB retired adaptive capacity (reactive) in favor of GAC (proactive global token buckets); waiting for throttling before reallocating is the named failure.

Routing/metadata caches whose miss behavior changes system load: DynamoDB's partition-map caching caused metastable failure risk; replaced with constant-work MemDS. Any cache on the request path must cost the same hit or miss.

Blocking or synchronous-global-membership DDL: F1 paper demonstrates naive distributed schema change corrupts data; trigger-based OSC is itself being retired at Meta/industry in favor of binlog/instant DDL approaches.
B-tree engines for write/space-bound flash fleets: Meta retired compressed InnoDB on UDB (kept 2x the storage and 4x the write traffic MyRocks needed).
Periodic-dump backups as the durability story: every hyperscaler moved to continuous log archival + per-second PITR; snapshot-only backup is a retired pattern.

Single-leader-for-the-whole-database designs (classic primary/standby) as the scale plan: every shared-nothing player shards consensus per range precisely because one Raft/Paxos group cannot scale writes or isolate blast radius.

Letting replication topology leak into the application (manual shard maps, client-side resharding): Spanner splits, DynamoDB partitions, and TiKV regions all split/move invisibly behind a routing layer; Meta's Akkio exists to make μshard placement invisible.

One bespoke clock assumption baked into commit protocol with no abstraction: CRDB's portability and AWS's later microsecond-clock retrofit show the winning designs treat clock quality as a pluggable bound, not a constant.
oyatie_prescriptions: Keep the ratified multi-Raft leader-per-range anchor unchanged — it is the proven convergence point of Spanner/DynamoDB/CRDB/TiKV/ZippyDB. Make the range the single unit of consensus, placement, split, repair, and CDC sharding. Target CRDB/TiKV-class defaults (range size in the 96–512MB band, split/merge automated, leaseholder serves consistent reads without full Raft round-trips).

Clock layer: implement an HLC with explicit uncertainty intervals behind a Rust ClockSource trait whose API is TrueTime-shaped (returns [earliest, latest], never an instant). Launch on NTP-grade sync with CRDB-style uncertainty restarts (max-offset class ~250–500ms); the same trait later accepts PTP/owned time fabric (AWS Time Sync proves microsecond bounds are commodity) to enable commit-wait external consistency without protocol rewrite. Do not buy atomic clocks for v1; do not hard-code their absence either.

Storage engine: bespoke Rust LSM with RocksDB-proven semantics (leveled compaction, column families, snapshots, ingest-external-SST for backfill/restore). Pebble is the precedent that a clean-room engine rewrite under a multi-Raft SQL layer works; MyRocks numbers (50% space, ~75% write-traffic reduction) are the economic justification. Add a TiKV-Raft-Engine-style dedicated multi-Raft log store so thousands of Raft logs don't thrash the main LSM WAL.

Wire the W5 CAS object store in as the log-archival + SST tier from day one: continuous Raft/redo log streaming to CAS gives per-second PITR with a 35-day window (DynamoDB/Aurora bar) as a property of the pipeline, not a backup job; SSTs in content-addressed storage make replica repair = fetch-by-hash (Aurora's 10s/10GB segment repair is the MTTR bar) and make backup/restore/branching cheap.

Build the placement driver as a separate consensus-backed Rust control service (TiKV PD / Spanner zonemaster / AutoAdmin analog): owns range splits/merges, heat-based rebalancing, lease transfers, and zone/cell topology. Integrate directly with the decided cell + shuffle-sharding doctrine: ranges never cross cells; the stateless routing tier is shuffle-sharded per tenant so a poison tenant blasts only its shard of routers.

Tenant isolation: implement DynamoDB's full progression in one step — per-range and per-router token buckets plus a proactive Global Admission Control service, with an RU-style normalized cost unit (read/write/storage) as the SaaS-facing currency. Split-for-heat must be automatic. Never ship static per-partition throughput allocation; it is the documented failure DynamoDB spent a decade unwinding.

Schema change: implement the F1 online asynchronous protocol (delete-only → write-only → backfill via ingest → public) in the SQL layer from the first DDL statement; CockroachDB's implementation is the open reference. Declare blocking DDL an admission-gate violation in the service's governance lane.

CDC as a schema object (Spanner model): change streams declared in DDL, change records written transactionally and co-located with the data write, stream shards that split/merge with ranges (DynamoDB Streams model), delivered over Pulsar as the launch-primary transport per /specs/api-contract-ssot-canonical.json. This is the platform primitive that feeds Oyatie search, caches, audit, and analytics — do not bolt it on later.

Control plane: strictly off the data path, cell-scoped, built on a deliberately simpler bootstrap metastore (single-Raft KV) before the distributed-SQL is self-hosting (Aurora-on-DynamoDB precedent). All routing metadata services must be constant-work (MemDS lesson) — same cost on hit and miss. Fleet operations (replica repair, leader rebalance, version rollout) are reconciliation loops, matching the k8s+Cluster API substrate already decided.

Quorum economics: support witness/log-only replica roles in the Raft implementation from the start (DynamoDB log replicas; Spanner witness replicas) — 3 full + 2 log-only style configs cut storage cost and heal quorums fast without full data copies.

Consistency surface: one strong default (serializable; external consistency when the clock bound permits) plus explicit read classes — follower reads, exact-staleness, bounded-staleness (Spanner read API shape; Cosmos's five levels prove the product demand, but its multi-master LWW mode is an explicit anti-goal for v1: no write-conflict resolution semantics in the SQL tier).

Adopt the predictability doctrine as an SLO contract: internal bars of P99 <10ms point read/write per range (Cosmos SLA bar; DynamoDB sustains single-digit ms at 146M req/s) authored as OpenSLO files at oya/<service>/slos/*.openslo.yaml per ADR-0130 before the service promotes past dev; latency SLOs gate promotion, not throughput benchmarks.

Engine-swap escape hatch: Google migrated Spanner's entire storage engine (SSTable→Ressi) online at >2B QPS — design the storage layer behind a versioned trait with dual-format ranges and per-range migration state in the placement driver so Oyatie can rev its LSM format fleet-wide without downtime.
