research.domain: Object/BLOB storage substrate (hyperscaler durability, metadata scaling, consistency, tiering, integrity verification) — feeds Oyatie W5 bespoke CAS object store

per_company.approach: PROVEN: 400+ trillion objects / exabytes / 150M req/s (Pi Day 2025; ~500T objects, 200M+ req/s per 2026 '20 years of S3' post), >1 PB/s peak across tens of millions of HDDs; >300 microservices in 4 planes: stateless REST front-end fleet, namespace/index service, storage (key-value node) fleet, storage-management background fleet. ShardStore (SOSP'21 best paper): bespoke append-only LSM storage node, ~40K lines of RUST, validated with lightweight formal methods — executable reference models + property-based testing on every commit, spec ~14% of code (vs 2-10x for full proofs), 16 bugs (incl. crash-consistency + concurrency) caught pre-production; maintained by non-FM-experts. Strong consistency RETROFIT (Dec 2020): kept the metadata cache (rejected disabling it — 'wouldn't meet our bar'), added CPU-style cache-coherence protocol + horizontally-scaled in-memory Witness service acting as per-object read barrier; verified with deductive proofs + model checking of runnable code ('more work than the implementation itself'); shipped default, free, no perf regression. Durability: 11-nines design target; erasure coding across ≥3 AZs (~5-of-9 / 1.8x overhead per re:Invent deep dives; hedged reads need any K of K+M); threat model centers software bugs + operator error, mitigated by human 'durability reviews' (security-threat-model style) + continuous background auditing with checksummed chain of custody; Dec 2024: default end-to-end integrity — CRC64NVME full-object checksum stored in metadata even for multipart, trailing checksums, SDK auto-validation. Heat: random + power-of-2-choices placement; workload decorrelation — a single customer burst spreads over 1M+ disks (drives stuck at ~120 IOPS since 2006 while capacity grew 7.2M-x); front-end load spread via DNS answers over a large endpoint fleet; multipart PUT + ranged GET are the official parallelism contract.

PROVEN: GFS successor; many multi-exabyte filesystems, two >10 EB each; largest clusters sustain >50 TB/s read / 25 TB/s write; busiest single cluster >600M IOPS; tens of thousands of machines per cluster. Architecture: rich client library (called 'most complex part' — software RAID, selectable encodings), curators = horizontally scalable control plane, METADATA IN BIGTABLE (gave >100x scale-up over largest GFS clusters; killed the GFS single-master) — and the famous recursion: Bigtable itself runs on Colossus, bootstrapped from a smaller instance; 'D' file servers (network-attached disks; data path is direct client<->D, no hops through control plane); custodians do background durability — disk balancing, RAID reconstruction. Placement: newly written data spread across all drives; ages/cools onto big HDDs; 'buy just enough flash to push I/O density into what disks provide.' L4 distributed SSD cache: index servers consulted before reads; ML-driven admission (CacheSack: insert on write / first read / second read); write-back mode advises curators to place new files on SSD then auto-migrate to HDD. GCS durability: 11 nines annual = data+code chunks (erasure coding) placed across multiple zones BEFORE write ack; 'data in transit within Cloud Storage is always checksum-protected, without exception'; Google states software bugs are 'potentially the single biggest risk to data durability' and 11 nines 'does not obviate the need to back up.'

PROVEN (SOSP'11, still the canonical design): storage stamps (cluster = blast radius, target ~70% utilization with headroom) + Location Service managing stamps/namespace; three co-designed layers — stateless front-end; partition layer (range-partitioned distributed table of objects, ranges split/merge/move by load, Paxos lock service); stream layer (append-only distributed FS: streams = ordered extents; 3-replica synchronous chain replication intra-stamp — write acked only after all 3; on failure, reconcile via minimum commit length; extents SEALED at target size). Strong consistency from day one — paper explicitly claims C+A+P for the partition types expected in a stamp; read-after-append identical from any replica. Erasure coding: lazy, background, on sealed extents only — Local Reconstruction Codes (ATC'12 best paper): LRC(12 data, 2 local, 2 global parity) ≈ 1.29x overhead vs 3x replication, with reconstruction reads needing only the local group (vs all fragments for Reed-Solomon); 3x -> 1.29-1.5x fleetwide. Geo: async inter-stamp replication with Location Service failover. Lesson in bundling: Blob+Table+Queue on one substrate proved one immutable-stream layer can host multiple data abstractions.

per_company.company: Meta (Tectonic + f4 + Haystack lineage — internal platform)
per_company.approach: PROVEN: f4 (OSDI'14) warm-blob tier: >65PB logical / 400B+ photos at publication; week-old blob request rate is ~10x lower than day-old, so heat-based tiering (photos migrate from Haystack after 3 months, other blob types after 1 month); RS(10,4) rack-aware in-DC = 1.4x, plus cross-region XOR of 'buddy' volumes = 2.1x effective replication vs Haystack's 3.6x; cell = 14 racks x 15 hosts x 30x4TB drives (6,300 drives); storage-less CPU-heavy 'backoff' nodes do online reconstruction and 'rebuilder' nodes do failure detection + background rebuild; assumes ~1% drive AFR. Tectonic (FAST'21): consolidated Haystack+f4+HDFS onto ONE exabyte multi-tenant FS per datacenter — reported cluster: 1250 PB at ~70% utilization, 10.7B files, 15B blocks; rationale: Haystack was IOPS-bound with stranded capacity, f4 capacity-bound with stranded IOPS — pooling fixes both. Metadata fully disaggregated, hash-sharded over ZippyDB KV in three INDEPENDENT layers (Name / File / Block) that scale separately; Chunk Store is flat and deliberately ignorant of files/blocks; fat client: single-writer-per-file write token, clients write directly to storage nodes; RS(9,6) with hedged 'reservation' requests (ask 19 nodes, use first 15) to dodge stragglers; tenant isolation via TrafficClass GOLD/SILVER/BRONZE + ephemeral resource sharing between latency-sensitive and background traffic.

PROVEN but thinner public record (First Principles engineering blog + docs): strong consistency FROM LAUNCH ('always serves the most recent copy... written to the system'); exceeds 11-nines durability — framed as <1 object lost per million over 10 years; redundancy across 3 availability domains (multi-AD regions) or 3 fault domains (single-AD regions); erasure coding among the storage schemes; engineering math starts from ~1% disk AFR => 'many disk failures every hour' at exabyte regional scale, countered by highly automated disk recovery completing in <30 MINUTES; 'data integrity is actively monitored using checksums, and corrupt data is detected and automatically repaired' (continuous scrub + self-heal, redundancy-loss triggers automatic re-copy). Tiers: Standard / Infrequent Access / Archive with auto-tiering. API limits: 10 TiB max object, multipart = 50 GiB max part, 10,000 parts max. No published equivalent of ShardStore/Colossus/Tectonic internals; differentiation is operational (fast recovery automation) rather than novel architecture.

convergent_patterns: Plane separation: every one of the five splits stateless front-end / scalable metadata-index plane / append-only data plane / background fleet-management plane (S3's 4 service groups; Colossus curators+Bigtable vs D vs custodians; WAS front-end/partition/stream + stream manager; Tectonic ZippyDB metadata vs flat chunk store; OCI implied by recovery automation). Metadata NEVER lives inside data nodes.

Metadata in a horizontally scalable sharded KV/DB — and the recursion is embraced: Colossus metadata in Bigtable (which runs on Colossus, bootstrapped), Tectonic metadata hash-sharded over ZippyDB, WAS partition layer is itself a range-partitioned database persisted in the stream layer, S3's namespace is its own massive replicated index subsystem. This is what retired the GFS-style single master and bought Google '100x' cluster scale.

Replicate-then-encode lifecycle: hot/incoming data is 3x synchronously replicated (often chain replication) for low-latency durable ack; data is sealed into immutable extents/volumes and LAZILY erasure-coded in background (WAS sealed extents -> LRC 1.29x; f4 locked volumes -> RS(10,4)+XOR 2.1x; S3 ~5-of-9 1.8x; Colossus selectable encodings; GCS data+code chunks across zones). Immutable/append-only sealing is the universal durability primitive — it makes EC, scrubbing, and repair tractable.

Locality-aware erasure codes that optimize RECONSTRUCTION cost, not just overhead: Azure LRC reads only a local group to rebuild; f4 keeps RS within a cell and uses cheap XOR cross-region; Tectonic hedges with 4 extra reservation nodes; S3 hedges reads needing any K of K+M. Convergence band: 1.29x–2.1x effective replication.

Durability is a continuously verified PROCESS, not a one-time math claim: background scrubbers/auditors re-checksum everything and auto-repair (OCI 'actively monitors... automatically repaired', disk rebuild <30 min; f4 rebuilder nodes; Colossus custodians; S3 continuous auditing + checksummed chain of custody), and the stated top threats are SOFTWARE BUGS and OPERATOR ERROR, not disks (Google: 'single biggest risk'; AWS durability reviews borrowed from security threat modeling).

End-to-end checksums at every hop plus a stored whole-object checksum: S3 made CRC64NVME full-object checksums the default for all new objects in Dec 2024 (works across multipart); GCS checksums all in-transit data 'without exception' and urges client-side verify; OCI checksums + auto-repair; WAS CRCs each append. Integrity is contract-level, not internal-only.

Strong read-after-write consistency is table stakes: Azure (2011), OCI, GCS designed it in; S3 had to retrofit it in 2020 with a witness/read-barrier + formally model-checked cache coherence. No one launched a major store with eventual consistency after 2011.

Heat management by statistical decorrelation, not per-object QoS: random + power-of-two-choices placement, spread new writes across the whole fleet, rely on millions of independent workloads smoothing aggregate load (S3 spreads one customer over 1M+ disks; Colossus spreads new data across all drives then migrates as it cools; f4/Haystack split by measured heat; Tectonic pools IOPS-bound and capacity-bound tenants).

Cell/stamp-scoped blast radius with a utilization ceiling: WAS stamps (~70% target), f4 14-rack cells, Tectonic per-datacenter clusters (also ~70% utilized), S3 AZ-spread shards, OCI AD/fault-domain triplets. Growth = add cells, not grow cells.
Multipart upload + ranged GET as the universal large-object parallelism contract (S3, OCI 50GiB parts/10K parts, Azure block blobs), with per-part checksums composing to a full-object checksum.

Tiering by access heat with published thresholds/automation (f4 3-month photo migration; Colossus L4 ML-driven SSD admission + auto SSD->HDD migration; S3 storage classes + Intelligent-Tiering; OCI auto-tiering Standard/IA/Archive).

Formal methods + Rust for the storage node is the proven modern path: ShardStore is ~40K lines of Rust validated by executable-spec property testing at ~14% code overhead, caught 16 production-grade bugs, maintainable by non-experts — and S3's consistency protocol was model-checked before launch. Direct, published precedent for bespoke-Rust storage at 11-nines grade.
divergences: Product shape: AWS/Azure/OCI ship the blob store AS the public API; Google and Meta run a general-purpose internal filesystem (Colossus, Tectonic) and layer object/blob products on top — filesystem-as-substrate lets one fleet serve blobs, warehouse, logs, and DB storage.

Client thickness: Colossus and Tectonic push EC, hedging, software-RAID, and even direct storage-node writes into rich trusted client libraries (single-writer write tokens); S3/Azure/OCI hide everything behind a thin HTTP contract because clients are untrusted. An owned full-stack (Oyatie) can use fat internal clients AND a thin public API.

Consolidation vs specialization: Meta consolidated three systems into one multi-tenant Tectonic cluster to pool stranded IOPS/capacity; AWS went the other way — 300+ specialized microservices and separate storage services. Both proven; the variable is org shape ('AWS ships its org chart').

Consistency origin: designed-in (WAS 2011 via commit-length chain replication; OCI; GCS) vs retrofitted (S3 2020 witness + cache coherence). The retrofit cost: verification work exceeding implementation work.

Geo-durability mechanism: f4 uses cross-region XOR coding (2.1x, synchronous durability); Azure/S3 use asynchronous geo-replication (RPO > 0); GCS offers dual/multi-region buckets with cross-zone EC. No consensus on sync-coded vs async-replicated geo tiers.

Metadata recursion strategy: Google runs metadata on Bigtable-on-Colossus (explicit bootstrap story); Meta uses a separate KV service (ZippyDB); Azure co-designed partition layer atop its own stream layer in-stamp; AWS built a bespoke index fleet. All scale; bootstrap/circularity handling differs.

SSD economics: Google published an ML-driven cache-admission layer (L4/CacheSack) as the answer to flash cost; AWS publicly leans on HDD decorrelation + power-of-two placement and sells SSD as a separate product (S3 Express One Zone). Meta tiers whole volumes by age instead.

Transparency of internals: AWS and Meta publish peer-reviewed system papers (SOSP/FAST/OSDI); Google publishes curated blogs only (no Colossus paper); OCI publishes least — claims must be weighted accordingly.
anti_patterns: Eventual consistency as the API default — S3's original design; explicitly retired in Dec 2020 because application workarounds (consistency-tracking layers customers built for EMR etc.) were worse than fixing the store. No post-2011 hyperscaler store shipped without strong consistency.
Single-master metadata (GFS master) — retired by Colossus moving metadata into Bigtable; the documented bottleneck that capped GFS cluster scale; bought >100x.

Workload-specialized storage silos — Meta retired Haystack+f4+HDFS into Tectonic because Haystack stranded capacity (IOPS-bound) while f4 stranded IOPS (capacity-bound); specialization without pooling wastes fleet.

Plain 3x replication for sealed/cold data — universally replaced by background erasure coding (1.29x–2.1x); but equally: inline EC on the hot synchronous write path is avoided — everyone acks on fast replication first (Tectonic's direct-RS warehouse writes are the deliberate exception for throughput tenants).
Disabling caches to win consistency — S3 explicitly rejected it ('wouldn't meet our bar for no tradeoffs on performance'); the proven move is a coherence protocol + witness, formally checked.

Trusting the durability math without continuous verification — all five treat 11-nines as a design target requiring scrubbers, auditors, auto-repair, and human review processes; Google explicitly warns software bugs are the biggest durability risk and 11 nines 'does not obviate backup'.

Global cross-tenant deduplication / exposing content addressing in the public object API — none of the five do it (they standardized on stored full-object CHECKSUMS for integrity instead); cross-tenant dedup creates timing/confidentiality oracles and correlated-loss blast radius.
Letting data nodes know about high-level abstractions — Tectonic's chunk store is deliberately ignorant of files/blocks; smart data nodes couple layers and block substrate reuse.
Growing one cluster/stamp without bound or running it hot — WAS and Tectonic both operate near ~70% utilization with headroom for rebuild + burst; full stamps are a documented operational hazard.

Testing-only correctness for storage nodes — S3 concluded conventional testing was insufficient at their scale and industrialized lightweight formal methods instead (and credits it with 16 prevented production issues).
oyatie_prescriptions: W5 CAS shape = the convergent four planes: (1) stateless axum front-end fleet, (2) metadata/index plane, (3) append-only chunk/extent data plane, (4) background fleet-management plane (scrub/repair/rebalance/tiering) as a first-class peer service. Enforce ADR-0132 single-concern: each plane is its own service under {cloud}/<service>/ with its own OpenSLO files.

Store W5 object metadata in the W5 bespoke distributed-SQL (multi-Raft leader-per-range) — this is literally Colossus-metadata-in-Bigtable / Tectonic-in-ZippyDB / WAS-partition-layer reapplied. Copy Tectonic's split: independent Name (bucket/key->object), Object (object->blocks), and Block (block->chunks/extents) keyspaces so each scales separately. Write the bootstrap ADR up front (small static-config seed instance, Google-style) because the recursion (SQL stores its own backup-store's metadata) is proven but must be explicit.

Strong read-after-write consistency from the first commit — designed-in (Azure/OCI/GCS path), never retrofit (S3 paid for it with verification work exceeding implementation). When a metadata cache is eventually added, require the S3 recipe as a governance gate: in-memory horizontally-scaled witness service as per-object read barrier + model-checked coherence protocol (stateright) BEFORE deploy. Strong consistency also unlocks conditional PUT (If-None-Match/If-Match), which the CAS and delivery fabric should expose day one.

Durability primitive = sealed immutable extents: 3x synchronous chain replication for the write ack (reconcile via minimum commit length on failure, per WAS), seal at target extent size, then background-encode sealed extents with a local-reconstruction code — start with Azure LRC(12,2,2) at 1.29x overhead (best published reconstruction-cost/overhead point) placed copyset-style across >=3 cells/fault domains. Never erasure-code inline on the hot path.

Content addressing is Oyatie's legitimate divergence — hyperscalers checksum but don't content-address publicly. Prescription: chunk IDs = BLAKE3 content hashes internally (serves buck2 content-addressed delivery fabric + integrity for free), but (a) ALSO store an S3-style full-object checksum (CRC64NVME-equivalent) in metadata composing across multipart parts, validated end-to-end on every hop; (b) scope dedup strictly per-tenant/per-cell — never cross-tenant (oracle attacks, correlated-loss blast radius — the reason no hyperscaler ships it); (c) refcount GC in the metadata plane, never in data nodes.

Build the continuous-verification plane before GA, not after: background scrubbers re-read and re-verify every extent checksum on a fixed cadence; redundancy-loss detection triggers automatic re-replication with an OCI-grade SLO (full disk rebuilt <30 minutes, sized from ~1% drive AFR); plus AWS-style human 'durability reviews' (threat-model format: risks + countermeasures documented separately) wired into the Oyatie governance pipeline as a required gate for any change touching the data plane. Threat model must rank software bugs and operator error above hardware.

Adopt the ShardStore methodology literally for the Rust storage node — it IS the founder doctrine's proof case (proven methodology, Rust-native): executable reference model + property-based testing (proptest/stateright) running on every commit in oya-ci, spec budget ~10-15% of node code, explicit crash-consistency checks (ShardStore's soft-updates-style dependencies), argument-by-bisimulation kept maintainable by non-specialists. Target: the published 40K-LOC-node scale is achievable by a small team.

API contract (axum surface): S3-compatible semantics as the floor — multipart upload (50GiB-class parts, 10K parts, per-part checksums composing to full-object checksum), ranged GET, strong consistency, conditional writes; internally serve reads from any K of K+M EC shards with hedged requests (Tectonic's reservation pattern: ask K+4, use first K) to cut tail latency.

Heat management by decorrelation, fused with the existing cell + shuffle-sharding doctrine: random + power-of-two-choices placement at PUT, spread new writes across the entire cell fleet, shuffle-shard tenants across chunk-server subsets so no tenant can heat a spindle set; tier by measured access heat with f4-style explicit thresholds (and leave an L4-style ML SSD-admission cache as a later, separately-shipped service — do not block W5 on it).

Tenant isolation inside the data plane: Tectonic TrafficClass (GOLD latency-sensitive / SILVER normal / BRONZE background) on every chunk-server request, with background scrub/rebuild/compaction always BRONZE and able to donate unused quota ephemerally; Cedar governs management-plane authz, but traffic-class enforcement is data-plane code — policy engines are too slow for the IO path.

Cells as stamps with a hard ~70% utilization ceiling (WAS + Tectonic concur): each storage cell owns its metadata ranges + chunk fleet + scrubbers; capacity growth = new cells admitted via Cluster API/Talos fleet automation; cross-cell placement only for the >=3-fault-domain EC spread. Per-cell SLOs ({cloud}/<service>/slos/*.openslo.yaml) before any promotion past dev, per ADR-0130.

Keep the chunk store dumb and flat (Tectonic's hardest-won lesson): chunk servers know chunks, checksums, and leases — nothing about objects, buckets, or tenants. This is what lets the SAME substrate later serve Pulsar tiered storage, distributed-SQL backups/snapshots, buck2 artifact CAS, and the delivery fabric — matching the universal hyperscaler endgame where the blob store becomes the substrate under every other stateful system.

research.domain: Compute substrate (VMs, containers/Kubernetes, serverless) across AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft Azure, Oracle OCI

per_company.approach: Borg (EuroSys 2015): one control plane ('Borgmaster', 5-replica Paxos) per cell, median cell ~10k machines, 99.99% control-plane availability, 10k+ task arrivals/min. High utilization via admission control (quota priced by priority band), task packing, overcommit, and machine sharing with process-level isolation. Priority bands: monitoring > production > batch > best-effort/free; production tasks never preempt each other (anti-cascade); quota deliberately oversold at lower bands (infinite free-tier quota). Resource reclamation runs ~20% of workload on slack reclaimed from prod limits; compressible resources (CPU/IO) throttled instead of killed. Quantified: segregating prod/non-prod would cost 20-30% more machines; per-user dedicated cells would need 2-16x cells; fine-grained requests vs bucketed sizes save 30-50% median. Scheduler scoring blends best-fit with E-PVM-style spreading to avoid stranding. Borg-next-gen (EuroSys 2020 trace): both CPU and RAM limits now allocated >100% of deployed capacity — statistical multiplexing as doctrine. Autopilot (EuroSys 2020): vertical+horizontal autoscaling from sliding-window percentiles + ML over job history; slack cut 46%→23%, OOM-impacted jobs reduced 10x; autoscaling-by-default. 'Borg, Omega, Kubernetes' (ACM Queue 2016): IP-per-pod, labels over job indices, choreographed small control loops over central orchestration. GKE: 65,000-node clusters (etcd replaced with Spanner-backed KV store), 130,000-node demonstrated 2025. GKE Autopilot: nodes fully managed, no SSH/no node ownership, per-pod per-second billing, 99.95% control-plane / 99.9% pod SLA. Isolation: gVisor (Sentry user-space application kernel) for GKE Sandbox and Cloud Run — recommended tier for SaaS running untrusted tenant code, 10-30% syscall overhead. COS: minimal immutable node OS. Spot VMs = monetized excess/reclaimed capacity, 30s preemption notice.

Nitro System: full virtualization offload — VPC, EBS, instance-storage controllers and host coordination on Nitro cards, hardware root of trust via Nitro Security Chip, minimal fixed-function hypervisor delivering bare-metal-indistinguishable performance; security whitepaper doctrine of no interactive operator (SSH) access to production hosts; enables .metal instances. Firecracker (NSDI 2020, written in Rust): minimalist VMM replacing QEMU for Lambda/Fargate; <5MiB memory overhead per microVM, boots to app code <125ms, 150 microVMs/s creation per host, thousands per host, jailer + seccomp-bpf defense in depth; moved Lambda from early per-customer dedicated EC2 instances to multi-tenant workers with per-function microVM isolation. Lambda container loading (USENIX ATC 2023): 10GiB images, scale-up to 15,000 containers/s, cold starts as low as 50ms via flattened images split into 512KiB content-addressed, convergent-encrypted chunks; deduplication (~80% of chunks shared across tenants), worker-local L1 cache + erasure-coded AZ-level L2 cache + S3 origin. SnapStart: encrypted Firecracker memory+disk snapshots restored in ~100-200ms (P90 cold invoke 1,681ms → 698ms). Placement: ML-driven placement service optimizing packing density while bounding noisy neighbors; stochastic fairness queuing + best-of-k placement with no shared state; deliberately co-locates dissimilar workloads (statistical multiplexing of anti-correlated demand). Firecracker 7-year lessons (Brooker 2025): snapshot cloning shares clean pages across VMs for memory density; prefer periodic VM recycling over complex memory reclamation; in-place CPU/memory grow-shrink makes ms-to-hours workloads economic. Bottlerocket: immutable dm-verity-verified container OS, API-driven config, no SSH/shell by default, image-based partition-flip updates, runs on EC2 and bare metal. Spot = monetized spare capacity pools, 2-minute reclaim warning.

Twine/Tupperware (OSDI 2020): ONE shared fleet doctrine — single regional control plane managing 1,000,000 machines, no clusters and no federation layer; all components sharded/scaled independently (scheduler sharded by entitlement; largest shard ~170k machines vs Kubernetes' ~5k-node ceiling). Entitlements: pseudo-clusters of dynamically allocated machines per business unit replacing static pools — machines are fungible, jobs move transparently across data centers. twshared grew 15% of fleet (Jan 2019) → 56% (Oct 2020) → ~85% target by early 2022. Host profiles: per-workload hardware/OS tuning (kernel version, HugePages, CPU settings) swapped dynamically when machines are reallocated; +11% web-tier performance. TaskControl API: applications collaborate in container lifecycle (e.g., ZooKeeper followers restart first, leader last) instead of opaque evictions. Small-machines doctrine: standardized single-socket 64GB nodes instead of SKU zoo — 18% power savings, 17% TCO savings; power is the binding datacenter constraint, fungibility beats per-workload hardware. Kubernetes-absence rationale: built before k8s matured; k8s per-cluster control planes strand capacity and add federation complexity; k8s lacked dynamic machine reallocation, host customization, and lifecycle collaboration at their scale. Runs containers (no VM layer) because the fleet is single-tenant first-party code — isolation ladder need is internal-trust, not hostile multi-tenancy.

Fabric Controller: per-cluster (~1,000 nodes) redundant control plane using 5-server Paxos-type replication; manages hardware lifecycle, health, and autonomic repair (reincarnates VMs on healthy servers on failure). Protean (OSDI 2020): the VM allocation service — single instance per availability zone covering 10k-100k machines; strict policy/mechanism separation with a flexible rule-based Allocation Agent; multi-layer caching gives millisecond allocation turnaround; achieves 85-90% on key packing-utilization metric; COVID capacity crunch absorbed by tweaking configurable validator-rule thresholds, not re-architecture. Resource Central (SOSP 2017): ML prediction system (VM lifetime, deployment size, CPU utilization percentiles) feeding allocator decisions including safe oversubscription of first-party workloads and lifetime-aware placement. AKS: node-centric managed k8s, ~5,000 nodes/cluster ceiling, forcing multi-cluster for larger fleets; Azure Linux as minimal container host. ACI: serverless container groups with Hyper-V isolation — every container group gets its own kernel (hypervisor-tier boundary chosen for multi-tenant serverless, not shared-kernel or user-space-kernel); standby pools of fully provisioned, initialized container groups auto-refilled to maxReadyCapacity for cold-start elimination. Azure Boost: Nitro-style offload of storage/networking to dedicated hardware. Azure Spot: spare-capacity monetization with eviction.

Bare-metal-first doctrine: launched industry-first cloud bare-metal instances; customer owns the whole server, zero hypervisor overhead. Gen2 off-box virtualization: network and storage virtualization removed from host software stack entirely and placed in an off-server Cloud Control Computer (CCC) — the host (even a compromised hypervisor or bare-metal tenant) physically cannot reach the control plane; VMs are layered on the same off-box substrate, so VM and bare-metal share one network/storage virtualization architecture. Acceleron converged NIC (2025): integrates host NIC + CCC on single silicon with hardware-enforced static isolation, targeting AI fleets. Trade-off accepted: less aggressive bin-packing/multiplexing than Borg-class schedulers in exchange for predictable performance and a hard tenant/control-plane trust boundary; VM, bare-metal, container instances, and OKE (managed k8s) all ride the same Gen2 substrate.

convergent_patterns: Hardware/off-box offload of virtualization: 4 of 5 (AWS Nitro cards + security chip, OCI CCC/Acceleron, Azure Boost, Google Titanium-class offload) moved network/storage/security virtualization off the host CPU onto dedicated hardware outside the tenant trust domain — host CPU sells compute, offload owns the trust boundary, bare-metal performance and bare-metal products fall out for free.

Shared-kernel containers are NEVER a hostile-tenant boundary: every hyperscaler running arbitrary multi-tenant code inserts a stronger boundary — Firecracker microVM (AWS Lambda/Fargate), Hyper-V per container group (Azure ACI), gVisor user-space kernel (Google Cloud Run/GKE Sandbox), full bare-metal/off-box separation (OCI). Plain runc is reserved for first-party trusted code (Meta's whole fleet, Borg, internal services).

One shared fleet with overcommit + priority tiers + reclamation, not per-team silos: Borg (20-30% machine tax if segregated; ~20% of workload runs on reclaimed slack; quota priced by priority band), Meta twshared (15%→56%→~85% of fleet), Azure Resource Central (ML-predicted oversubscription), and all of AWS/Google/Azure monetize the same reclaimed slack externally as Spot/preemptible with 30s-2min reclaim notice.

Minimal, immutable, API-driven, zero-SSH node OS: AWS Bottlerocket (dm-verity, partition-flip A/B updates, no shell), Google COS, Azure Linux, plus Nitro's no-operator-access doctrine and GKE Autopilot/ACI removing node access entirely — node as cattle reached via API only. Direct validation of Talos-style OS.

Snapshot/restore + chunked content-addressed distribution + warm pools for cold-start: Lambda (512KiB convergent-encrypted dedup chunks, L1 worker/L2 AZ erasure-coded caches, 50ms starts, 15k containers/s), SnapStart (100-200ms microVM restore), Firecracker snapshot cloning with clean-page sharing, Azure ACI standby pools, GKE/Cloud Run min-instances — all converge on 'pay init cost once, restore many, cache in tiers'.

Predictive/ML layer on top of reactive autoscaling and placement: Google Autopilot (slack 46%→23%, 10x fewer OOM kills, ML + sliding-window percentiles), Azure Resource Central (lifetime/utilization prediction feeding allocator), AWS Lambda ML placement (packing density + noisy-neighbor bounds). Manual resource limits treated as the failure mode.

Control-plane scale via sharding and scoped domains, never federation: Borg cells (~10k machines), Protean per-AZ (10-100k), Twine sharded single regional plane (1M, largest shard 170k), GKE 65k nodes by replacing etcd with a Spanner-backed store. Nobody ships a federation layer over many small control planes.

Allocator engineering pattern: policy/mechanism separation with rule pipelines (Protean), hybrid scoring that mixes best-fit packing with spreading to avoid capacity stranding (Borg E-PVM hybrid), best-of-k sampling with no shared state for noisy-neighbor bounds (Lambda), multi-layer caching for millisecond placement decisions at 85-90% utilization (Protean).

Application-collaborative lifecycle instead of opaque eviction: Twine TaskControl (leader-last restarts), Borg SIGTERM-with-deadline + maintenance windows, k8s PDB/graceful-drain lineage — stateful systems must get a callback into fleet maintenance ordering.
divergences: Isolation-tier choice for multi-tenant code: AWS bet on hardware virtualization minimized (Firecracker microVM, ~125ms boot, <5MiB overhead); Google bet on a software user-space kernel (gVisor, 10-30% overhead, better density/compat tradeoff); Azure bet on full Hyper-V per container group (heaviest, most conservative); OCI bet on physical separation (bare metal + off-box control). No consensus on the middle of the ladder — only on its floor (never shared-kernel) and ceiling (hardware root of trust).

Fleet topology: Meta runs ONE regional control plane over 1M machines with no cluster concept; Google runs many ~10k-machine Borg cells per site; Azure scopes allocation per-AZ (Protean) over ~1k-node fabric clusters; AWS never exposes an internal fleet-manager equivalent publicly. Cell size doctrine ranges 1k → 1M.

Hardware homogeneity: Meta standardized on one small SKU (single-socket 64GB; 18% power, 17% TCO savings) for fungibility; AWS/Azure/Google run enormous heterogeneous instance-type zoos because they sell the SKUs; OCI leans into large dedicated bare-metal shapes.

Kubernetes posture: Google created and operates it at 65k-130k nodes; Azure/AWS offer managed k8s with ~5k-node ceilings; Meta rejected it outright (scale, stranded capacity, host customization); OCI treats OKE as one product among bare-metal-first primitives.

Serverless capacity strategy: AWS engineers cold starts away with snapshots + content-addressed loading (no standing capacity per function); Azure pre-provisions standby pools (pay for warmth); Google Autopilot reframes the problem as per-pod billing on a managed fleet.

Memory management for long-lived microVMs: AWS DSQL deliberately recycles VMs on a timer ('simplicity wins') while Aurora Serverless tracks page-access frequency — even within one company the complex and simple approaches coexist by workload.
anti_patterns: Per-team / per-workload dedicated machine pools and clusters — Meta spent 2019-2022 actively retiring siloed pools into twshared; Borg paper quantifies segregation at 20-30% extra machines and dedicated per-user cells at 2-16x cell count. Stranded capacity is the named enemy.
Federation layers over many small control planes — Twine explicitly forgoes clusters and federation; Google scaled the single GKE control plane (etcd→Spanner-backed store) rather than federate.

QEMU as the serverless VMM — AWS evaluated and rejected it (attack surface, footprint), building Firecracker in Rust instead; early per-customer dedicated EC2 workers for Lambda were also retired in favor of Firecracker multi-tenant workers.
SSH/interactive operator access to production hosts — Nitro has no operator access mechanism by design; Bottlerocket ships no shell; GKE Autopilot and ACI remove node access from customers entirely.
Shared-kernel containers as a hostile-tenant boundary — no hyperscaler does this anywhere arbitrary tenant code runs.
Manual resource-limit setting as the default — Google measured manually-managed jobs at 46% slack vs 23% autopiloted and 10x more OOM-impacted jobs; manual limits are the legacy path.
Preemption within the production priority band — Borg forbids prod-preempts-prod to prevent preemption cascades.

In-host-kernel/hypervisor network virtualization consuming host CPU — retired across AWS (Xen dom0 → Nitro), OCI (off-box from day one), Azure (Boost); it burns sellable cores and puts the control plane inside the blast radius.
Pure best-fit bin-packing — Borg rejected it (strands capacity, punishes burst); production scoring blends packing with spreading.
Complex memory reclamation machinery when periodic recycling suffices — Firecracker/DSQL lesson: fixed-lifetime VM recycling 'naturally cleans up built-up cruft'.
etcd as the datastore at extreme cluster scale — GKE replaced it with a Spanner-backed KV store to reach 65k nodes.
oyatie_prescriptions: One shared fleet, never per-team clusters: adopt Borg/Twine doctrine directly. Cells of 5-10k nodes are the control-plane scaling unit (matches decided cell-based + shuffle-sharding architecture); add a Twine-style 'entitlement' abstraction — a Rust service that dynamically carves machine quota per product lane out of one fungible fleet, with Cluster API moving machines between cells. Per-team clusters are a quantified 20-30% capacity tax; reject them in ADR form now.

Codify the isolation ladder as policy (Cedar-enforced at the workload-admission gate): Tier 0 — first-party Oyatie Rust services: hardened runc/containerd pods on k8s (seccomp, cgroups, no tenant code). Tier 1 — anything executing tenant-influenced code (SaaS plugins, queries, functions): Firecracker microVM per tenant workload. Firecracker is already production-proven Rust (Apache-2.0); per founder doctrine this is the rare case where 'reimplement Rust-native' means adopt-and-fork the proven Rust artifact, integrating via a bespoke Rust orchestrator (kata-style runtime shim for k8s). Tier 2 — bespoke distributed-SQL and CAS object store data planes: dedicated bare-metal cells (OCI doctrine: stateful data plane gets hardware predictability and a physical trust boundary). Never let shared-kernel containers cross a tenant boundary — zero hyperscalers do.

Talos-style zero-SSH OS is unanimously validated — go further: immutable dm-verity-verified root, image-based A/B partition-flip updates, API-only management (Bottlerocket pattern), no shell in the image at all, plus Twine 'host profiles': declarative per-cell kernel tunables (HugePages, scheduler, NIC settings) applied when a machine is re-entitled, owned by the Cluster API provider. Twine measured +11% from host profiles alone.

Implement Borg's economic model in the scheduler: four priority bands (system/monitoring > prod > batch > best-effort), quota priced by band, oversold/free at the bottom; resource reclamation runs batch on slack reclaimed from prod requests (~20% free capacity at Google); compressible resources (CPU) throttle, non-compressible (RAM) kill; prod never preempts prod. buck2 CI builds and batch analytics are the natural best-effort consumers — this is Oyatie's internal spot market and the single highest-ROI utilization lever.

Autoscaling: vertical-first, predictive-over-reactive (Borg Autopilot). Build a Rust rightsizing recommender consuming the ADR-0130 observability/SLO substrate: sliding-window percentile + decay-weighted history sets CPU/memory requests per service; target <25% slack fleet-wide; manual limits require an annotated exception. Layer reactive HPA beneath it. Publish slack and OOM-kill rate as fleet SLOs.

Unify the delivery fabric: ONE content-addressed substrate (the planned bespoke CAS object store) serves buck2 build artifacts, OCI container images, AND microVM snapshots — exactly the Lambda architecture (512KiB convergent-encrypted chunks, dedup across tenants ~80%, worker-local L1 + cell-level erasure-coded L2 cache, origin in object store). This collapses three delivery systems into one and is the proven path to 50ms-class cold starts with 10GiB images at 15k containers/s.

Cold-start engineering for the functions/jobs runtime: snapshot-restore over boot (SnapStart pattern — init once per version, restore 100-200ms), clean-page sharing across cloned microVMs for memory density, small warm standby pools per cell (ACI pattern) auto-refilled; recycle long-lived microVMs on a fixed timer instead of building memory-reclamation machinery (Brooker simplicity lesson).

Allocator (Rust, per cell): Protean's policy/mechanism separation — declarative rule pipeline for constraints, multi-layer caching for millisecond placement; scoring blends best-fit with spreading (Borg hybrid) to avoid stranding; best-of-k sampling with stochastic fairness queuing for noisy-neighbor bounds without shared state (Lambda pattern); deliberately co-locate anti-correlated workloads. KPI: Protean-class 85-90% packing utilization, published on the SLO substrate.

Predictive placement layer (Resource Central analog): predict workload lifetime and peak utilization from history; permit oversubscription only for first-party (Tier 0) workloads, never tenant-facing microVMs. Feed predictions into the allocator as soft scores, hard rules stay declarative.

Lifecycle collaboration API (TaskControl analog): a gRPC/Rust-trait callback contract letting Pulsar brokers, distributed-SQL range leaders, and other stateful services sequence their own restarts (followers-first, leader-last) during node drains and fleet maintenance — implemented as a maintenance-orchestration k8s controller above PodDisruptionBudgets.

Control-plane datastore escape hatch: keep cells ≤10k nodes today; the proven path past etcd limits is GKE's etcd→Spanner move — plan for kube-apiserver backed by the bespoke distributed-SQL (W5 destination) as the scale-up route, never federation.

Homogeneous hardware doctrine: standardize on 2-3 node shapes per cell maximum (Meta small-machines: 18% power / 17% TCO savings); fungibility multiplies shuffle-sharding entropy and entitlement flexibility. Resist a SKU zoo — Oyatie sells SaaS, not instance types.

Offload trajectory for the owned kernel/OS: structure virtio device backends and CNI/storage data planes so they are pinned to dedicated host cores outside the tenant trust domain now, and can migrate to DPU/off-box hardware later (Nitro/CCC/Boost convergence). Design rule: the substrate control plane must remain reachable-from-host=false even under hypervisor compromise (OCI's bar).

research.domain: Billing + Metering + Tax + FinOps + Capacity (hyperscaler doctrine: AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft Azure, Oracle OCI)

per_company.approach: Metering measured per-second, rated hourly, invoiced monthly: EC2/EBS per-second billing since Oct 2017 (60s minimum, Linux). Canonical billing artifact is CUR/Data Exports: CUR 2.0 has 125 fixed columns grouped Bill/Identity/LineItem/Pricing/Product/Discount; each line item carries identity_line_item_id + identity_time_interval; the open month is continuously restated and frozen at invoice. SKU model = (service, usage_type, operation) tuple against versioned public price lists. Marketplace metering (the externalized doctrine): BatchMeterUsage required, AWS dedups per product/customer/hour/dimension, records older than 6 hours rejected, sellers told to verify transmission via CloudTrail — seller bears accuracy responsibility. AWS Billing Conductor = productized pro-forma RE-RATING engine: same usage re-rated under custom pricing plans (rule precedence global → billing-entity → service → SKU) + flat/percentage custom line items; each billing group computes as its own consolidated-billing family with its own RI/SP sharing and volume tiers. Savings Plans = hourly dollar commitment denominated in SP rates, applied AFTER RIs, EC2-Instance-SPs before Compute-SPs, allocated highest-discount-percentage-first each hour, owner account first then shared accounts, remainder billed on-demand; SP charges appear as hourly line items (covered-usage + negation pattern in CUR). Internal ledger: FLASH (Financial Ledger & Accounting Systems Hub) migrated off Oracle (185 instances, 93 DBs, 120 TB, 20+ years of SOX/audit financial data) to DynamoDB with S3 as immutable audit trail of journal changes — 40% latency reduction, 70% cost reduction. SaaS Architecture Fundamentals doctrine: METERING (bill-generating events) is architecturally separate from METRICS (operational analytics). FOCUS-format Data Exports supported (announced FinOps X 2024).

Cloud Billing exports to BigQuery as the canonical FinOps surface: standard table + detailed resource-level table (gcp_billing_export_resource_v1_<ACCOUNT>) with per-resource cost rows; FOCUS BigQuery view + Looker template. Committed Use Discounts in two species — resource-based and spend-based — with documented benefit-attribution modes: proportional attribution (GA) lands commitment fees+credits in the same rows/time as eligible usage so net cost is always accurate at read time; prioritized attribution alternative. Budgets are explicitly NOT caps: docs state budgets never stop consumption; hard-stop requires programmatic billing-disable via Pub/Sub notification, or API quota caps — enforcement lives in quota, not billing. Internal capacity economics (Borg, EuroSys'15): quota = vector of resource quantities at a given priority for a period (typically months); quota check is admission control at job submission, not scheduling; higher-priority quota COSTS MORE, quota allocation handled outside Borg and tied directly to physical capacity planning with price/availability varying per datacenter; priority-0 best-effort is effectively free/infinite. This is the published archetype of internal capacity markets driving team discipline.

No external billing; capacity itself is the internal currency and accountability unit. RAS — Resource Allowance System (SOSP'21): continuously optimized region-wide datacenter resource allocation; abstracts heterogeneous hardware via Relative Resource Units (RRUs) normalizing CPU/memory/flash/GPU performance differences, giving services guaranteed capacity entitlements. Twine (OSDI'20) does cluster/container management beneath it. Global Reservations Service: latency-tolerant services request ONE global reservation instead of per-region quotas; system auto-sizes disaster-readiness buffers (request 300 servers → 450 provisioned across 3 regions, 150 spare). Flux (OSDI'23): fully automated top-down capacity regionalization — RPC-tracing-derived service capacity models feed a joint capacity+traffic optimization plan spanning thousands of services, tens of products, millions of servers, tens of regions, continuously orchestrated rebalancing. ~14+ datacenter regions. Accountability model per public sources is capacity-quota/reservation grant + ownership transfer (capacity-as-budget), not dollar chargeback — forecasting and entitlement replace invoices.

Internal Commerce platform (one platform behind Azure, M365, Marketplace) spans catalog, subscription, metering/rating, billing, and revenue-recognition components; Microsoft migrated it onto Azure itself (Inside Track). The publicly specified contract is Marketplace metering service — the cleanest published usage-event spec anywhere: exactly ONE usage event per resource per dimension per calendar hour (accumulate intra-hour client-side), events accepted only ≤24h old else Expired, duplicate = 409 Conflict echoing the originally-accepted event, batch max 25 with per-event status (Accepted/Expired/Duplicate/ResourceNotFound/ResourceNotActive/InvalidDimension/InvalidQuantity/BadArgument), dimension identifiers IMMUTABLE once offer published, ≤30 dimensions/offer, included-quantity locked post-publish, and a reconciliation API exposing reconStatus ∈ {Submitted, Accepted, Rejected, Mismatch} comparing submitted vs processed quantities. Cost Management ships FOCUS-format exports. Capacity: Protean (OSDI'20) VM allocation service at global scale sustaining 85–90% on a key utilization metric incl. COVID capacity-crunch adaptations; Resource Central (SOSP'17) collects VM telemetry, learns behavior offline, serves online predictions to resource managers via client library; both with public trace releases.

Commercial model built on Universal Credits rather than per-SKU commitments: Annual Flex = committed dollar pool of credits consumable against ANY eligible OCI service in ANY region at discounted rates (analyst-documented discount bands from low-double-digit % at ~$100K/yr commits to ~70% at ~$10M/yr); credits expire at end of each annual service period, unused amounts forfeited and nonrefundable, no rollover by default; Pay As You Go bills monthly at list with no commitment; BYOL bridges on-prem licenses. Spend flexibility is the selling point: hourly/daily/monthly burn can vary within the annual dollar commit. Cost and usage reports delivered as files to Object Storage; OCI supports FOCUS-format billing exports and published a prebuilt function converting historical reports to FOCUS — smallest published billing-internals surface of the five, but full convergence on the FOCUS interface.

convergent_patterns: Metering is a pipeline, not a query: at-least-once event collection → idempotent dedup keyed on (customer/resource, dimension, time-window) → windowed aggregation → deterministic rating → invoice. AWS Marketplace dedups per product/customer/HOUR/dimension; Azure rejects duplicates per resource+dimension+calendar-hour with 409; GCP/OCI aggregate to SKU-hour line items. The HOUR is the universal rating/aggregation window across all five even when measurement is per-second.

Measurement granularity is finer than rating granularity, which is finer than invoicing granularity: per-second measurement (EC2 since 2017, 60s minimum; GCP per-second), hourly rated line items, monthly invoices. Decoupling these three clocks is the doctrine.

Bounded lateness + explicit rejection: every published metering API imposes a hard late-event window (AWS Marketplace 6h, Azure 24h) and returns explicit Expired/Duplicate statuses rather than silently absorbing or double-counting — accuracy bar is 'reject and reconcile', never 'best effort accept'.

Versioned immutable price catalog with locked SKU identity: SKU = stable tuple (AWS usage_type+operation; Azure dimension identifier immutable post-publish; GCP SKU IDs; OCI rate card). Price changes are new catalog versions; rating = pure function of (raw usage, price-book version), which is exactly what lets AWS Billing Conductor re-rate identical usage under pro-forma custom price books.

Open-month restatement, invoice-time freeze, post-close corrections as new line items: CUR restates continuously until invoice; GCP export updates until invoice with CUD proportional attribution keeping net cost accurate; corrections after close are credit/debit memo line items — line items are append-only, identified (identity_line_item_id), never mutated.

Commitment discounts are rating-time benefit ALLOCATION over the same usage line items, not separate metering: AWS SP hourly-commitment greedy allocation (highest-discount-first, after RIs, owner-account-first sharing), GCP CUD proportional/prioritized attribution, Azure reservations/savings plans, OCI credit drawdown — all emit explicit covered-usage/negation/credit line items so the discount math is auditable in the export.

FOCUS (FinOps Open Cost & Usage Spec) is the converged external schema: AWS, Microsoft, Google, and Oracle all ship FOCUS-format exports; FOCUS 1.2 (ratified 2025-05-29) adds SaaS columns — pricing currencies, EffectiveCost/ContractedCost, credits/tokens as non-monetary pricing units, ServiceProvider vs HostProvider split.

Quota/admission-control enforces, billing observes: Google docs state budgets never cap usage; Borg quota check is admission control priced by priority and tied to physical capacity planning; Meta grants capacity entitlements (RAS RRUs, reservations) before workloads run; AWS service quotas are separate from billing. No hyperscaler puts spend enforcement inside the billing pipeline.

Internal capacity economics replaces (or precedes) dollar chargeback and drives dogfood discipline: Google sells priced quota internally (higher priority = higher price), Meta allocates capacity-as-currency via reservations/RRUs with forecasting (Flux: millions of servers, thousands of services), Azure runs prediction-driven allocation (Resource Central telemetry → Protean allocator at 85–90% utilization). Capacity accountability is structured as forecast → entitlement → measured consumption.

Financial truth is an append-only double-entry subledger with automated verification, separate from the rating pipeline: Amazon FLASH (SOX, 20+ years, 120TB, S3 immutable audit trail of journal changes), Microsoft commerce rev-rec component, Stripe Ledger as the published state-of-the-art (5B events/day, 99.99% of dollar volume verified within 4 days, 99.9999% money-movement explainability via balance-state-machine + data-quality platform).

Tax is a determination engine at a clean seam, never inlined in rating: jurisdiction resolved from customer evidence (country/state/postal, geolocation), calculation invoked at invoice/checkout finalization, registration-threshold monitoring runs as a separate concern (Stripe Tax, Avalara AvaTax pattern; hyperscalers likewise compute tax downstream of rating, per-invoice).
divergences: Commitment-model shape: AWS = hourly rate-commitments (SP/RI) with greedy per-hour allocation; GCP = dual resource-based + spend-based CUDs with selectable attribution modes; Azure = hybrid (reservations + savings plan + MACC contract commits); OCI = prepaid expiring dollar pools (Universal Credits, annual forfeiture). OCI's is the simplest to implement; AWS's is the most expressive and most complex to rate.

Export substrate: GCP lands billing data natively in its own warehouse (BigQuery tables, queryable immediately); AWS and OCI deliver files (Parquet/CSV to S3/Object Storage); Azure exports to storage + API. GCP is the only one treating the warehouse as the primary billing interface.

Multi-price-book re-rating sits at different layers: AWS productized it in-platform (Billing Conductor pro-forma billing groups); Microsoft pushes it to Partner Center/CSP price lists; GCP leaves it to resellers — only AWS exposes the re-rating engine itself as a service.

Meta and Google internal models differ on the currency: Google prices quota in (internal) money by priority band — a true internal market; Meta allocates physical-capacity entitlements (RRUs, server reservations) with ownership transfer and no published dollar chargeback — budget-as-machines vs budget-as-priced-quota.

Accuracy responsibility boundary in marketplace metering: AWS makes the seller responsible for delivery (verify via CloudTrail, 6h window); Azure provides a platform-side reconciliation API (reconStatus Submitted/Accepted/Rejected/Mismatch) — Azure publishes the strongest reconciliation contract, AWS the strongest seller-liability doctrine.

Hard spend caps: none of the five offers a true hard billing cap on general usage; GCP documents the gap explicitly and offers programmatic billing-disable; Azure has spending limits only on credit subscriptions; AWS has none. The industry answer is quota-side caps, not billing-side.
anti_patterns: Billing off the observability/metrics pipeline: AWS SaaS doctrine explicitly splits METERING (invoice-grade, bill-generating) from METRICS (operational analytics) — one pipeline serving both is the canonical failure mode.

Mutable usage records or editable SKU/dimension definitions post-publication: Azure locks dimension identifiers and included quantities at publish; CUR line items are identified and append-only; corrections are new line items (credit/debit memos), never UPDATEs.
Unbounded late-event acceptance: every published API enforces a lateness window (6h AWS, 24h Azure) and an explicit Expired rejection — open-ended event ingestion makes invoice close impossible.

Trusting client-side aggregation without reconciliation: Azure ships a recon API precisely because submitted vs processed quantities drift (Mismatch is a first-class status); AWS instructs CloudTrail-based verification.

Monolithic vertically-scaled RDBMS as the financial ledger: Amazon retired Oracle-based FLASH (185 instances, 120TB, 10%/yr cost growth, interlocked components blocking scaling) for a purpose-built journal store + immutable object-store audit trail.

Budgets/alerts as enforcement: GCP documents that budgets never stop consumption; enforcement belongs in quota/admission control (Borg rejects at submission), and conflating the two produces either outages or runaway bills.

Synchronous per-request billing writes on the hot path: every external contract is batched (BatchMeterUsage mandatory; Azure batch ≤25; accumulate-then-emit per hour) — rating is asynchronous downstream of a buffer.

Inventing a bespoke cost schema then mapping to standards later: all four public clouds converged on FOCUS after years of incompatible exports (CUR vs BigQuery export vs Cost Management vs OCI reports) — the divergence is now acknowledged legacy cost.

Bottoms-up manual capacity regionalization: Meta explicitly retired per-region, service-owner-driven capacity asks in favor of top-down automated global planning (Flux) and single global reservations — per-team regional spreadsheet capacity is the named anti-pattern.
oyatie_prescriptions: Ship oya/metering as a single-concern flat µservice (ADR-0132) with an axum batch ingestion API → Pulsar topic (launch-primary per /specs/api-contract-ssot-canonical.json) → idempotent sink in bespoke distributed-SQL. Dedup key = (tenant_id, resource_id, dimension, usage_hour_utc) unique index + client idempotency_key; on duplicate return Azure-style 409 echoing the originally-accepted record. At-least-once everywhere upstream, exactly-once effect at the sink.

Adopt FOCUS 1.2 as the INTERNAL canonical usage/cost schema from day one (Oyatie already cites it): ChargeCategory/ChargeClass, BilledCost/EffectiveCost/ContractedCost/ListCost, SkuId, PricingUnit, CommitmentDiscount* columns reserved now, ServiceProvider/HostProvider. Add tenant_id and cell_id as first-class tag dimensions so per-tenant-per-cell cost attribution (cells + shuffle-sharding economics) is native, not a join.

Three-clock doctrine: measure per-second (60s minimum, EC2 pattern), rate hourly (the universal aggregation window), invoice monthly. Enforce a 6-hour lateness window (AWS Marketplace bar) with explicit Expired rejection status; never silently absorb late events.

Versioned immutable price book in the bespoke distributed-SQL: SKU identity = (service, usage_type, operation); price-book versions append-only with effective_from; published SKU/dimension identifiers immutable forever (Azure locking rule). Rating engine = pure deterministic function (raw usage × price_book_version) → line items, which gives Billing-Conductor-class pro-forma re-rating (custom tenant price books AND internal chargeback) from one engine for free.

Line items are append-only and identified: ULID line_item_id + usage_time_interval (CUR identity columns pattern); open billing period restates continuously; invoice close freezes the period; post-close corrections are new credit/debit memo line items. Build the close process before launch — restatement-then-freeze is the auditability bar.

Implement the accounting PRD as an append-only double-entry subledger now, in the bespoke distributed-SQL, with the debits=credits invariant enforced transactionally per journal entry (multi-Raft leader-per-range makes per-tenant journal ranges natural). Copy Stripe Ledger's verification doctrine: model money movement as a balance state machine and run an automated data-quality lane targeting ~100% of usage-dollars reconciled ingestion→rated→invoiced→ledger within days (Stripe: 99.99% of dollar volume within 4 days, 99.9999% explainability). Archive every journal mutation to the bespoke CAS object store as the immutable audit trail (FLASH S3 pattern; SOX/K-GAAP-grade).

Revenue recognition shapes the ledger schema: per ASC 606/IFRS 15, model performance obligations explicitly — deferred-revenue account per subscription obligation recognized ratably, metered usage recognized as delivered; rev-rec is a read of the subledger, not a separate system (Stripe Revenue Recognition pattern: automatic allocation across metered + recurring billing models).

Tax = bespoke-Rust SEAM, not a bespoke tax-content engine: a TaxCalculator trait with (a) jurisdiction resolution from customer evidence (country/region/postal, Stripe Tax pattern), (b) versioned rate/rule tables as data, (c) calculation invoked only at invoice finalization, (d) background registration-threshold monitoring. Ship two providers day one: KR VAT native (10% destination-based on SaaS; Simplified Business Operator Registration via NTS Hometax within 20 days of first sale; quarterly filing by the 25th; no input-VAT credit under simplified scheme; 1% non-registration penalty since 2024-01-01) and EU non-Union OSS (single member-state registration, quarterly return at destination rates). Keep an Avalara/Stripe-Tax adapter slot behind the same trait for US sales tax later — per founder doctrine, tax CONTENT is the one thing never to reimplement.

Quota enforces, billing observes — hard boundary: spend enforcement lives in the Cedar-policied per-cell quota/admission service (Borg pattern: quota check at admission, priced by priority/reservation class); budgets are alerts plus an optional automated-suspend action (GCP billing-disable pattern). Never put caps inside the rating pipeline.

Dogfood via internal chargeback from W1: every oya/* and cloud/* service gets a billing account and flows through the SAME metering→rating→ledger pipeline (Google priced-quota + Meta capacity-entitlement doctrine). Express capacity grants in normalized resource units (RAS RRU pattern) per cell; shuffle-sharded cell costs roll up through FOCUS tags so cell economics gate promotion alongside SLOs (ADR-0130 alignment).

Commercial model sequencing: launch with on-demand + OCI-style prepaid credit pools (committed dollar pool, discount bands, annual expiry — simplest correct commitment model); defer AWS-style hourly Savings-Plans allocation (highest-discount-first greedy over hourly line items, applied after any reserved commitments) until the rating engine is stable — it is pure rating-time logic over the same line items, so reserving FOCUS CommitmentDiscount columns now costs nothing.

Expose reconciliation as a product API: per-tenant usage-event status endpoint with reconStatus ∈ {Submitted, Accepted, Rejected, Mismatch} comparing submitted vs processed quantities (Azure contract), and write the metering audit trail to the CAS object store so tenants and auditors can verify (CloudTrail-verification pattern).

Capacity planning W5+: prediction-driven, not market-driven, at Oyatie's scale — per-cell telemetry → peak-demand forecasts feeding quota issuance tied to the physical capacity plan (Resource Central → Protean → Borg-quota chain); record Flux-style global joint capacity+traffic optimization as a future ADR, not a now-build.

research.domain: Messaging / Eventing / Streaming substrate (queue vs log vs bus taxonomy, multi-tenant broker isolation, exactly-once reality, schema governance, saga doctrine, DLQ/replay, ordering, event-driven metering)

per_company.approach: Four-product taxonomy, each single-concern: SQS (work queue: at-least-once, visibility timeout, DLQ+redrive; FIFO variant adds MessageGroupId per-group ordering + MessageDeduplicationId with 5-minute dedup window marketed as 'exactly-once processing'); SNS (fan-out notification, FIFO variant with topic- or group-scoped dedup); EventBridge (event bus: rules/pattern-matching routing, schema registry with auto schema-discovery in OpenAPI3/JSONSchema, archive+replay with replay-name metadata tagging, per-target DLQ, 256KB payload cap driving claim-check pattern via S3); Kinesis Data Streams (partitioned log: shard = 1MB/s write + 2MB/s read + 1000 rec/s, MD5(partition-key)->shard, On-Demand mode auto-splits shards exceeding 500KB/s within 15min, defaults to 200MB/s scaling to double the trailing 30-day peak). PROVEN scale: SQS peaked at 166M messages/sec Prime Day 2025 (86M/s 2023, 70.5M/s 2022). Builders' Library queue doctrine (Yanacek): never expose raw queues — wrap behind authenticated APIs; heartbeat the visibility timeout for long work or suffer cascading 'fork-bomb' redelivery brownouts; alarm on oldest-message-age; sideline unprocessable backlogs; per-tenant fairness throttling inside shared queues. Saga doctrine (Prescriptive Guidance): orchestration via Step Functions for complex/compensating flows (5+ steps, conditional logic), choreography via EventBridge for simple reactive flows, hybrid is normal.

Single converged Pub/Sub service: topics/subscriptions are GLOBAL resources, publish anywhere/consume nearest-region; per-message parallelism — service leases individual messages instead of partition assignment, explicitly rejecting partition-based scaling; 99.95% monthly-uptime SLA. Exactly-once delivery GA but REGIONAL only (guarantee holds when subscribers connect in one region; cross-region subscribers can see duplicates); ordering keys give per-key publish-order delivery (also regional) and exactly-once+ordering requires in-order acks; seek/snapshot for replay/backfill. Eventarc is the bus layer, delivering CloudEvents-format over HTTP. Decisive negative datapoint: Pub/Sub Lite — the zonal, partition-based, provisioned-capacity variant — was deprecated (closed to new customers Sep 2024, full shutdown June 30 2026) with migration guidance to Pub/Sub (ordering-key + autoscaling model) or Managed Service for Apache Kafka. Google is the only hyperscaler that collapsed queue+bus into one global service and it killed its own partitioned product.

Internal split mirrors queue-vs-log: Scribe (log bus) + FOQS (priority work queue), with the Async tier composing both. Scribe (VLDB'25 paper, 18-year evolution): multi-tenant buffered log; >15TB/s ingest, >110TB/s served to consumers (2019 blog: 2.5TB/s in / 7TB/s out); millions of producers, hundreds of thousands of categories and consumers; write path = local Scribed daemon (memory+disk buffering) or direct Write Service batching by category; storage on LogDevice partitions, retention 'a few days'; deliberately BEST-EFFORT delivery — small loss accepted to preserve throughput/latency, with opt-in configs trading performance for lower loss; only 'rough' ordering (~30min storage-timestamp window) — precise ordering pushed to stream processors (Stylus); multi-tenancy via rate limits, quotas, autoscaling, consumer buckets. Tulip schematizes petabytes/day flowing over Scribe. FOQS: multi-tenant distributed priority queue on SHARDED MYSQL (item = row: namespace, topic, 32-bit priority, 10KB payload, delivery delay), trillions of queue operations/day, thousands of topics per namespace, evolved regional->geo-distributed for disaster-readiness. Async tier learnings: Submitter (validation + overload protection) -> FOQS -> Dispatcher -> compute; 'delay tolerance' as first-class scheduling dimension (ms to days); workloads spike 0->millions exec/sec; consumption rates range 10s/min to 10M+/min per topic.

Deliberate, documented 3-product split (Microsoft Learn 'Compare messaging services'): Service Bus = enterprise MESSAGES ('priceless' payloads — orders, payments) with sessions (SessionId -> exclusive-lock ordered FIFO per session), transactions spanning entities, duplicate detection (MessageId-based, default 10-min window, configurable 20s–7 days), DLQ subqueue, Premium geo-DR + geo-replication; Event Hubs = partitioned append LOG for telemetry/streaming (Throughput Unit = 1MB/s or 1000 ev/s ingress, 2MB/s egress; up to 40 TUs/namespace standard; auto-inflate; Kafka-compatible endpoint; Capture offloads segments to Blob/ADLS — tiered storage in product form; millions of events/sec); Event Grid = discrete EVENT router (push delivery, per-subscription filters, CloudEvents 1.0 native). Published taxonomy rationale: an event is a lightweight notification of state change where the consumer decides what to do; a message carries an expectation of guaranteed processing — this events-vs-messages distinction is the doctrinal basis of the split. Microsoft states billions of CloudEvents are raised and handled daily across Microsoft Cloud.

Replicates the AWS 4-way taxonomy with smaller published limits: OCI Streaming (Kinesis-shaped partitioned log, now with Kafka-compatible APIs; partition = 1MB/s write / 2MB/s read — identical unit economics to a Kinesis shard; stream pool acts as root of a virtual Kafka cluster for tenancy scoping); OCI Queue (SQS-shaped serverless queue: at-least-once, visibility timeout 0s–12h default 30s, DLQ after configurable 1–20 delivery attempts, retention 10s–7d, 256KB max message, 'channels' — up to 256 ephemeral sub-destinations per queue for filtering/request-response/fairness, 10MB/s ingress+egress per queue, 100k in-flight cap, no ordering guarantees documented); OCI Events (EventBridge-shaped rules bus, CloudEvents-format per Oracle docs); OCI Notifications (SNS-shaped fan-out). OCI is the cleanest evidence that the AWS taxonomy is the convergent reference architecture: a second-mover independently shipped the same four shapes with the same delivery contracts.

per_company.company: Yahoo / Apache Pulsar lineage (ratified Oyatie substrate)
per_company.approach: Yahoo built Pulsar (open-sourced 2016) because no existing system supported millions of topics + native multi-tenancy + geo-replication + cursor management + stable performance under backlog; Kafka lacked all of these then. Yahoo production: 100B+ messages/day, 1.4M topics, <5ms average publish latency. Architecture: stateless brokers over BookKeeper bookies — ledgers split into immutable segments replicated (default 3 bookies) by the broker acting as client; bookies separate journal disk from entry-log disk so read spikes (backlog drain) cannot degrade write latency; sealed segments offload transparently to object-store tiered storage while clients still read the backlog; metadata in ZooKeeper (now pluggable; Oxia direction). Tenancy is first-class: tenant -> namespace -> topic hierarchy with namespace-level publish/dispatch/subscribe rate quotas, per-tenant authn/authz, bookie-affinity groups pinning a namespace's persistence to specific bookies, broker isolation policies; stateless brokers let noisy tenants be rebalanced without moving data. Unified queue+stream via subscription types: Exclusive/Failover (stream), Shared (work queue), Key_Shared (key-ordered work queue). Built-in per-topic schema registry with server-side enforcement; built-in retry-letter + dead-letter topics (Shared/Key_Shared; incompatible with transactions — use negative-ack there); transactions API for exactly-once consume-transform-produce within Pulsar. PROVEN third-party scale: Tencent Midas billing platform runs tens of billions of financial transactions/day on Pulsar at 99.999% availability with <10ms per-transaction budgets, having rejected Kafka on consistency/durability grounds and RocketMQ — events-as-billing-source proven on exactly this substrate. Honest cost: heaviest ops burden in class — brokers + bookies + metadata quorum (+ RocksDB inside BookKeeper) is 3–4 stateful subsystems vs Kafka's one.

convergent_patterns: Queue/log/bus trichotomy is the convergent product taxonomy: AWS (SQS/Kinesis/EventBridge+SNS), Azure (Service Bus/Event Hubs/Event Grid), OCI (Queue/Streaming/Events+Notifications), and Meta internally (FOQS queue vs Scribe log, Async tier choosing between them). The three shapes have distinct contracts — work queue = per-message lease + visibility timeout + DLQ; log = partitioned, offset-addressed, replayable, retention-bounded; bus = schema-described discrete events, rules/filter routing, push delivery. Google is the partial exception (one global Pub/Sub) and even Google ships Eventarc as a bus and Managed Kafka as a log.

At-least-once + idempotency is the universal ground truth; every 'exactly-once' claim is scoped: SQS/SNS FIFO = 5-minute dedup window; Service Bus = MessageId dedup window (20s–7d); Pub/Sub = exactly-once delivery only intra-region; Kafka/Pulsar transactions = only within the broker's own transaction domain. All five converge on dedup-token publish + idempotent consume, with the transactional outbox (+ inbox/idempotent consumer) as the actual cross-system enterprise answer — no provider offers end-to-end exactly-once across heterogeneous boundaries.

Ordering is only ever offered per key/group/partition/session, never global: SQS FIFO MessageGroupId, Kinesis partition key (MD5->shard), Pub/Sub ordering key (regional), Service Bus SessionId, Event Hubs partition key, Pulsar Key_Shared/partition key, Meta Scribe explicitly refuses precise ordering (~30min rough window) and delegates it to stream processors. Key choice = tenancy/aggregate identity is the standard prescription.

DLQ + bounded delivery attempts + redrive/replay is a mandatory contract on every product: SQS DLQ+redrive, EventBridge per-target DLQ + archive/replay (replayed events tagged with replay metadata), Service Bus DLQ subqueue, OCI Queue DLQ (1–20 attempts), Pub/Sub dead-letter topics + seek/snapshot, Pulsar retry-letter + dead-letter topics. Replay mechanics split by shape: logs replay via offset/cursor/seek, buses replay via archive, queues redrive from DLQ.

Compute/storage disaggregation + segment/tiered storage won: Pulsar/BookKeeper segments offloading to object store (2016), Kafka capitulated via KIP-405 tiered storage (GA, KRaft-only), Event Hubs Capture to Blob/ADLS, Kinesis On-Demand abstracts shards entirely, Scribe stores on LogDevice with days-scale retention and offloads durability to the warehouse. Broker-local-disk-as-system-of-record is dead at scale.

Schema registry attached to the substrate with enforced compatibility evolution: Confluent SR (BACKWARD default, transitive modes, consumer-first upgrade ordering for backward compat), EventBridge schema registry + automatic schema discovery, Pulsar built-in per-topic registry with server-side enforcement, Azure Schema Registry in Event Hubs, Meta Tulip schematizing petabytes/day over Scribe. Contract-first eventing (AsyncAPI as the EDA analogue of OpenAPI) is the governance overlay.

Multi-tenant fairness inside shared brokers via quotas + rate limits + throttling + tenant rebalancing: Pulsar namespace quotas/bookie affinity/broker isolation, Scribe per-category rate limiting + quotas + autoscaling, SQS fairness throttling for multi-tenant queues (Builders' Library), Event Hubs throughput units, OCI stream pools as tenancy roots. Logical isolation primitives must exist IN the broker, not just around it — validating the Pulsar-over-Kafka choice.

CloudEvents 1.0 as the cross-vendor event envelope: CNCF-graduated (Jan 2024), native in Azure Event Grid, Google Eventarc, OCI Events, Alibaba EventBridge; Microsoft reports billions of CloudEvents/day in production.

Backlog operations doctrine: alarm on oldest-message-age (not depth), heartbeat/extend visibility for long-running work to prevent redelivery storms, sideline poison/backlog traffic to quarantine queues, classify workloads by delay tolerance (Meta: ms to days) and schedule accordingly, protect ingestion with admission/overload control (Meta Submitter, AWS wrapping queues behind authenticated APIs).

Saga doctrine: orchestration (Step Functions / Durable Functions / internal workflow engines) for complex compensating multi-step flows; choreography over the bus for simple reactive fan-out; hybrid per-flow choice; never distributed 2PC across services.

Autoscaled/serverless capacity beats user-provisioned partitions: Kinesis On-Demand (auto shard-splitting, scales to 2x trailing peak), Pub/Sub never exposed partitions, Pub/Sub Lite (provisioned/partitioned) deprecated, Event Hubs auto-inflate, SQS serverless since 2006. Per-partition unit economics converged at ~1MB/s write / 2MB/s read (Kinesis shard = OCI partition = Event Hubs TU).

Events as the metering/billing source with a no-loss tier: AWS SaaS lens — tenant-activity billing events aggregated into invoices, Marketplace MeterUsage hourly per dimension per customer, accuracy/no-drop as an explicit design condition; Tencent Midas runs tens of billions of billing transactions/day over Pulsar at 99.999%; contrast with Scribe's explicit best-effort tier — hyperscalers run TWO loss classes: lossy/cheap telemetry vs never-lose money/audit paths.
divergences: Google vs everyone: single global-by-default service with per-message parallelism (individual message leases, no partitions) vs partition/shard-based regional products at AWS/Azure/OCI. Google's bet trades per-key throughput ceilings and regional-only ordering/EO guarantees for operational simplicity and global topology.

Meta vs cloud vendors: Scribe is openly BEST-EFFORT (bounded loss accepted for 15TB/s+ ingest economics) — no public cloud sells a lossy tier; and FOQS builds a trillions-ops/day priority queue on sharded MySQL rather than purpose-built log storage, prioritizing leverage of a hardened storage substrate over bespoke engines.

Product-count split: Azure deliberately ships 3 products with a published events-vs-messages doctrine, AWS ships 4+, OCI copies 4, Google collapses to ~1.5 (Pub/Sub + Eventarc), Pulsar unifies queue+stream in one system via subscription types. The taxonomy is convergent but whether it surfaces as separate PRODUCTS or separate MODES of one substrate is contested — Pulsar and Google prove single-substrate works.

Storage coupling: Pulsar disaggregated broker/storage from day one (BookKeeper segments); Kafka spent a decade broker-coupled and only converged via KIP-405 tiered storage + KRaft; Meta separated transport (Scribe) from storage (LogDevice) similarly. Direction of travel is uniform but Kafka's installed base still mostly runs coupled.

FIFO mechanics: AWS uses message-group IDs with throughput-scoped dedup; Azure uses sessions with exclusive consumer locks; Pulsar uses Key_Shared dispatch; Pub/Sub uses ordering keys with in-order ack requirements — same per-key guarantee, four incompatible APIs.

Priority as a first-class queue dimension: only Meta FOQS exposes per-item 32-bit priority + delivery delay; no public-cloud queue offers true priority queues (AWS doctrine: use separate queues per priority class).
anti_patterns: Partitioned, provisioned-capacity 'lite' tiers: Google deprecated Pub/Sub Lite outright (closed Sep 2024, shutdown June 30 2026), migrating users to autoscaling ordering-key Pub/Sub — direct retirement of the partition-provisioning model.

External coordination quorums as broker metadata: Kafka removed ZooKeeper entirely (KRaft default, ZK code deleted in Kafka 4.0); Pulsar community moving to pluggable metadata / ZooKeeper-less (Oxia) for the same reason — a separate consensus cluster is retired industry-wide.

Global/total ordering across a system: nobody offers it; Meta explicitly retired precise ordering from the bus (rough ~30min ordering, push exact order to stream processors); all providers cap ordering at key/session/partition scope.

Claiming end-to-end exactly-once across heterogeneous systems: Kafka transactions stop at the cluster boundary; 2PC between broker and application database is explicitly rejected as impractical — every primary source lands on outbox + idempotent consumers instead.

Unbounded retries without deadline awareness: the SQS 'fork-bomb' — workers running past visibility timeout cause parallel redelivery cascades and brownouts; Builders' Library mandates stop-at-expiry or heartbeating.
